articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Nine killed and dozens wounded in Russian strikes as Kyiv braces for harsh winter
articles.body:
- 
  Russian airstrikes killed nine people, injured dozens and damaged buildings and infrastructure across Ukraine on Saturday, as Kyiv braces for a “very difficult” winter amid intensified attacks on the country. The civilian death toll has risen sharply in Ukraine over the past two months as Russia steps up attacks on power plants and other infrastructure. Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia, and both sides have targeted each other’s shipping.
- 
  Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, writing on Telegram, said Russia had deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since early morning. “Basically, the Russians have expanded the war away from the front, where they have no success, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war,” he wrote. “Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance.”
- 
  The city council in Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine’s frontline “fortress cities” that Russia wants to capture, said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period. Four people were injured. “These are not military targets,” the council said. “They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business.”
- 
  The governor of Ukraine’s Zhytomyr region, Vitaliy Bunechko, said a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zviahel, west of Kyiv. Bunechko said two petrol stations also came under attack.
- 
  Earlier, Zelenskyy reported attacks on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, his home town. The governor of Zaporizhzhia region, Ivan Fedorov, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities.
- 
  In Odesa region, governor Oleh Kiper said 37 people, including an infant, were injured in a series of overnight attacks, while two people were missing. Russia’s defence ministry said Russian forces have maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, hitting a cargo ship in Odesa that it said was carrying goods for military use.
- 
  Ukrainian officials said the country was bracing for a brutal winter as intensified Russian attacks on infrastructure and key export industries compound a deepening budget crisis. The economy minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko, said damage to infrastructure and fixed assets from Russian airstrikes was estimated at close to $10bn this year, while the broader economic costs of the attacks and the de facto blockage of its ports had cut 1.5 percentage points of GDP. “We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country,” he said.
- 
  With fighting on the frontline largely stalled, Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted logistics networks and other economic assets in an effort to undermine each other’s war effort. For more than two weeks, Russia has carried out near constant attacks on Kyiv using faster jet-powered drones, disrupting life, business and government operations. Moscow has also effectively blocked Ukraine’s Black Sea ports by intensifying its air attacks on the country’s southern regions. Ukraine’s main exports – agricultural products and iron and steel – are shipped via these ports.
- 
  In Moldova on Ukraine’s western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed.
- 
  Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami for talks on ending the war, in a media interview released Saturday, but the Kremlin immediately ruled it out. “It is impossible,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told AFP in New Delhi on Saturday, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting can only take place in the Russian capital. The gathering of world leaders takes place on 14-15 December and there has been no confirmation yet as to whether Putin would attend. Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face meeting with Zelenskyy.

articles.title: Russian Nuclear Head Says Ukraine Attacked Fuel Trucks, Endangered Zaporizhzhia Plant
articles.body:
The head of Russia's state nuclear energy corporation accused Ukraine on Sunday of attacking diesel fuel trucks, killing two Russian servicemen and deliberately jeopardizing safety at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Ukraine.
Alexei Likhachev said the attack took place on Friday and also resulted in injuries to other Russian soldiers.
The Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe's largest with six reactors, was seized by Russian forces in the early weeks of the Ukraine war that broke out in February 2022. Each side has regularly accused the other of actions that endanger safety at the plant and increase the risk of a nuclear accident.
Likhachev issued a statement saying Ukrainian forces had launched “a series of combined strikes” on Friday on fuel trucks which deliver diesel to the station.
“The strikes hit very close to the perimeter of the station's site,” he said.
“Two servicemen were killed, and a large number of Russian soldiers were injured, some seriously. They were all involved in supporting this purely civilian mission.”
Fuel is critically important for the plant as diesel generators provide power to keep nuclear fuel in the reactors cool when the plant's two external power links are down. Both were down for nearly three weeks in August and September.
Ukraine has demanded that Russia abandon the station and hand its operation back to Kyiv, a demand rejected by Moscow. The fuel currently generates no electricity.
The UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, has stationed an observer team permanently at the station, along with Ukraine's three other working plants.
The agency has repeatedly acted as an intermediary when disputes arise and last month helped arrange a local ceasefire in order to carry out repairs and restore external power links.
Russia Hits Truck Near Polish Border in Latest Strike Near NATO
Russia attacked a truck near Ukraine's border with Poland, Polish and Ukrainian officials said on Sunday, the latest strike to hit areas near NATO as Moscow and Kyiv intensify their long-distance strikes to try to shift momentum in the war.
Polish border guards told Reuters that the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack around 800 meters (half a mile) from Poland, but that the crossing has since resumed operations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in Western Ukraine. Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.
Russia has begun targeting Ukraine's border crossings with its Western allies in recent weeks, part of a growing campaign by both sides to erode the other's economic infrastructure more than four years into Russia's invasion.
India and China Offer to Help Broker Peace
In India, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had been attending the BRICS summit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had offered help brokering a peace settlement, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Last month, at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Modi told Putin that the war must end, one of several calls for peace by leaders of nations that have traditionally strong relations with Russia.
Last month, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly told Putin that he should halt the conflict along the front line, which has remained largely static this year.
Russia has ruled that out, saying Ukraine should pull back to leave the industrialized eastern Donbas region in Moscow's hands, something Kyiv has said it will never do.
Both Brazil and China, themselves founding BRICS members, have called for a resumption of peace talks.
TASS cited Peskov as saying that Putin had informed Modi of the situation “on the ground” in Ukraine, and that Russia had not ruled out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October.

articles.title: Drones attack oil refineries in Russia's Tatarstan – photo, videos
articles.body:
Drones attack oil refineries in Russia's Tatarstan – photo, videos
Drones attacked the industrial zone of Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan on the night of 12-13 September, where major Russian oil refineries are located.
Source: monitoring Telegram channels; Russian media outlet ASTRA
Details: Local residents reported hearing drones flying over the city overnight, followed by a series of explosions.
Witnesses also reported that Russian air defence systems were active near an industrial area.
Local authorities have not yet reported the extent of possible damage to processing facilities or any casualties.
Nizhnekamsk is home to one of the Russian Federation's largest oil-refining hubs. The attack targeted facilities that play a key role in financing the war and supplying the Russian military with fuel.
In particular, the TANECO oil-refining and petrochemical complex is among the five largest oil refineries in Russia, with a designed crude oil processing capacity of more than 16 million tonnes per year. The refinery is one of Russia's main producers of diesel fuel, aviation gas for fighter jets and petrol for cars.
Another major oil refinery, TAIF-NK, is located nearby. The plant can process more than seven million tonnes of oil and gas condensate annually. TAIF-NK specialises in the production of petrol, diesel and other petroleum products. Its products are actively supplied both to the domestic Russian market and for the needs of the Russian forces.
Another facility in the Nizhnekamsk industrial zone is Nizhnekamskneftekhim, part of the Sibur petrochemical holding company and one of Europe's largest petrochemical plants. The plant is effectively a monopoly in Russia for the production of many types of synthetic rubber and plastics.
Background:
- Nizhnekamsk is located more than 1,200 km from Ukraine's state border.
- This is not the first attack on strategic oil-refining facilities in the region. In August 2026, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported a successful strike on the TANECO oil refinery.
- In addition, in early July, a Ukrainian strike drone captured on surveillance cameras fell on the neighbouring TAIF-NK plant in the Nizhnekamsk industrial zone.
- On 10 August, drones attacked Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Tatarstan, where an oil refinery is located.

articles.title: Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train
articles.body:
Ukraine, Poland say Russia hit Warsaw-bound passenger train
September 13, 2026
Russia launched two drone strikes on western Ukraine, close to its border with NATO member Poland, Ukrainian and Polish authorities said on Sunday.
One of the drones hit a locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn railway station in the Volyn region., some two kilometers (1.24 miles) from the border crossing.
"The monitoring team gave the train crew advanced warning, and thanks to that, no one was injured," Ukrainian railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in online post.
Separately, Poland's PKP Intercity confirmed that they have taken control of the affected train following the attack in the Ukrainian territory.
"The train is carrying 206 people. There are no Polish citizens among the passengers," the operator said online. "After completing customs clearance, it will continue its journey towards Warsaw."
Senior Western figures said to be at station before train strike
Ukrzaliznytsia later said that senior Western figures, including Boris Johnson and former CIA Director David Petraeus, were at the station shortly before the Warsaw-bound train was struck.
"Shortly before the locomotive was hit at the Ukrainian-Polish border, a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station," Ukrzaliznytsia said in a statement.
"There were, among others, security advisers from several EU member states and former European leaders on board, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson. In another train that was at Yagodyn station at the very moment of the attack was former CIA Director David Petraeus."
Johnson didn't specifically mention that he had been near the vicinity of the attack, but called for more action to be taken against Russian President Vladimir Putin, once reports of the attack emerged.
"I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning," Johnson said.
"When are we going to give them the air defences they need? Why won’t we unfreeze Putin’s cash and give it to Ukraine? There is more than €140 billion ($163 billion) in a Belgian bank account — and about £10 billion (€11.7 billion or 13.5 billion) in London," Johnson said, adding that Britain could lead the way in this regard.
"This wasn’t our train, but the one just minutes after us by the border crossing. It was evacuated as the drone approached and no one was hurt," Carl Bildt, Sweden's former Prime Minister said on X.
Poland says attacks on its territory cannot be ruled out
Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski urged for increased support for Ukraine, calling the incident an "escalation."
"This is an escalation, this is another great challenge for Ukraine and for the hypothetical future victims of Russian aggression and this means that we should double our efforts to support victims of aggression," Sikorski told a press briefing.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting on Sunday to address Russian drone attacks near the border and warned the country must be prepared for the possibility that drones could target Polish territory.
"The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side," Tusk said, adding Poland "cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory."
Zelenskyy: Locomotive 'deliberately burned'
On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the locomotive was "deliberately burned" and a gas station damaged in Volyn.
"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," he said.
Moscow did not immediately comment on the reports.
Ukrainian officials also reported another drone strike on Yahodyn overnight, some half a mile (800 meters) from the Polish border.
The border with Poland serves as essential transit point for military and humanitarian aid.
'Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors' — Ukrainian foreign minister
Commenting on the Yahodyn incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric" attacks were more than "just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."
"This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he said in an English-language post on X.
He urged Ukraine's Western allies to make Russia "feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex."
"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level," he added.

articles.title: Hollywood-style PR cannot mask Washington’s strategic defeat in Iran skies
articles.body:
Hollywood-style PR cannot mask Washington’s strategic defeat in Iran skies
TEHRAN — The administration of US President Donald Trump has increasingly resorted to Hollywood-style public relations campaigns in a desperate bid to manufacture a false sense of victory over Iran, seeking to gloss over the catastrophic failure of its military adventurism against the Islamic Republic.
Washington’s latest attempt to engineer a cinematic narrative out of an operational humiliation came to light after a CNN report revealed that the Pentagon pressured two US Air Force crewmen—whose F-15E Strike Eagle was shot down deep within Iranian territory—to participate in a curated interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes.”
According to the report, the two airmen initially resisted the media stunt, expressing grave reservations that they were effectively being coerced into participating by top political brass. However, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and other high-ranking political appointees at the Pentagon aggressively pushed for the broadcast to sanitize the reality of the battlefield.
CBS noted that the airman who ultimately agreed to appear—identified only by the callsign “Bravo”—was the downed aircraft’s weapons systems officer, holding the rank of colonel, who spent roughly two days stranded alone in the rugged Iranian terrain. CNN acknowledged that the coercive push exposes how Hegseth and the Trump administration have been maneuvering to manipulate the narrative surrounding an increasingly unpopular and costly war with Iran, using a sensationalized survival tale to distract from severe military setbacks.
The incident stems from the downing of the multi-million-dollar F-15E Strike Eagle on April 3, following the unprovoked military aggression launched by the United States and Israel on February 28.
The precision interception of the advanced US warplane by Iran’s indigenous air defense networks delivered a profound strategic blow to the Pentagon, shattering the long-promoted myth of Western aerial supremacy over sovereign Iranian airspace. The downing demonstrated the high readiness and lethal accuracy of Iran’s integrated defense umbrella, forcing Washington into a chaotic and vulnerable posture.
Both crew members ejected from the doomed aircraft. While the pilot was extracted in the immediate hours following the crash, the weapons systems officer remained trapped deep inside Iranian territory for over 36 hours as US forces mounted a high-risk rescue operation under the constant threat of Iranian tracking.
Far from the heroic triumph Washington’s PR machine is attempting to market, the rescue mission itself nearly devolved into a catastrophic debacle reminiscent of past American military misadventures in the region.
Two US transport aircraft dispatched to extract the airman and special operations personnel became immobilized at a remote airstrip. Facing imminent capture and exposed to Iranian reconnaissance, US forces said they were forced to scuttle and blow up their own stranded aircraft to prevent advanced military hardware and sensitive technology from falling into the hands of the Iranian Armed Forces, before scrambling replacement planes to complete the evacuation.
Political analysts view the Pentagon’s orchestration of the 60 Minutes broadcast as a textbook diversionary tactic. By shifting public attention toward the individual survival drama of a stranded officer, Washington hopes to divert Western public scrutiny from the broader strategic failure that, despite billions of dollars in military expenditure, US assets remain acutely vulnerable to Iran’s deterrence capabilities.
As Washington’s military objectives hit a solid wall of Iranian resistance, the Trump administration’s reliance on manufactured heroics only underscores the growing gap between Pentagon propaganda and the harsh realities of the battlefield.

articles.title: Over the past day, more than 200 combat engagements took place on the front line — the General Staff provided details

Over the past day, more than 200 combat engagements took place on the front line — the General Staff provided details
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces launched 2 missile strikes and 63 airstrikes, dropped 228 aerial bombs, and carried out more than 2,000 attacks. The hottest area is the Pokrovsk direction.

Details
It is noted that the enemy launched two missile strikes, carried out 63 airstrikes, and dropped 228 guided aerial bombs.
In addition, it deployed 6,477 kamikaze drones for attacks and carried out 2,046 shelling attacks on settlements and the positions of our troops
Situation by direction

In the Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces halted three attempts by the invaders to advance near Zakitne, Yampil, Mykolaivka, and Rai-Oleksandrivka; another attack is ongoing.

russia is suffering significant losses at the front, while the average life expectancy of a new recruit after arriving on the battlefield may be between 20 and 30 minutes. articles.title: Modi-Xi's Ukraine offer to Putin, strong message to West & new Brics playbook: Key outcomes of summit
articles.body:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers opening remarks at the Brics Summit Session on 'Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth' at Bharat Mandapam, on Day 2 of the 18th BRICS Summit, at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Sunday. (@MEAIndia X/ANI Photo)
NEW DELHI: The 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi brought together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for two days of high-level diplomacy, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi holding key bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.The summit saw a renewed push to stabilise India-China ties, a reaffirmation of the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussions on the West Asia crisis, Ukraine, maritime security, trade and energy. Alongside formal negotiations, images of PM Modi with Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian projected a strong message of engagement and unity within the expanded grouping.The summit also featured informal diplomatic moments, including PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex, leaders attending a gala dinner featuring a specially curated Indian menu, and a symbolic Banyan tree plantation highlighting India's emphasis on sustainability and interconnectedness.The two-day summit also produced a series of initiatives covering agriculture, health, technology, startups, energy, urban mobility, supply chains, skilling and global governance. The New Delhi Declaration, adopted after intensive negotiations, provided the summit's principal political outcome, covering terrorism, conflicts, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.
PM Modi-Xi meeting signals push to stabilise ties
PM Modi and Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, with both leaders stressing the need to view India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.
The two sides expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and said the relationship should be guided by mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.The leaders also discussed maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border, economic and trade relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. Both sides underlined the need to address each other's concerns and facilitate meaningful and predictable market access.Also read: 'Have opportunity to discuss cooperation': PM Modi welcomes Xi; bilateral talks beginPM Modi also thanked China for its support and cooperation during India's Brics chairship and conveyed best wishes to China as it prepares to assume the Brics chairship next year.Xi said China and India should continue to approach their relationship from a strategic perspective and keep long-term bilateral development in mind. He also stressed the importance of cooperation between the two major Global South countries.
Modi-Putin talks focus on Ukraine, West Asia
PM Modi and Putin held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing major regional and global developments.The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to assist peace efforts.Also read: Modi-Xi-Putin bonhomie, car diplomacy, gala dinner, Pahalgam condemnation and New Delhi Declaration: Brics Summit key takeawaysThe discussions covered defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia also agreed to work towards increasing bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030 and discussed implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030.Putin invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit, with dates to be finalised through diplomatic channels.
Putin car ride becomes summit highlight
One of the most closely watched visual moments came after the Modi-Putin meeting, when the two leaders travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.The image underlined the longstanding India-Russia relationship at a time of continuing geopolitical tensions surrounding Moscow and highlighted India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.Also read: PM Modi, Putin share car ride again in Delhi, weeks after traveling together in Bishkek - watchPM Modi also presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar."Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.
Kremlin says PM Modi, Xi offered help on Ukraine
Russia said PM Modi and Xi offered their "good offices" to help find a solution to the Ukraine conflict during their separate interactions with Putin on the sidelines of the summit.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin welcomed their readiness, saying: “During their bilateral meetings, Modi and Xi took a keen interest in the Ukraine settlement and actively offered their good offices to help find a solution,”.The development came amid continuing international efforts to find a settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war.
PM Modi-Pezeshkian talks centre on West Asia
PM Modi also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with the discussions focusing on India-Iran ties, Brics cooperation and the escalating conflict in West Asia.PM Modi reiterated India's consistent position that disputes should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region. The two leaders also discussed freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers amid disruptions to shipping routes.The meeting followed their earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. India has also stressed the need to expand and diversify bilateral trade channels with Iran.
Iran-UAE engagement amid regional tensions
Pezeshkian also held talks with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the summit.The meeting was significant as Iran and the UAE have had differences over regional security, while Gulf states maintain varying degrees of security cooperation with Western powers.Their interaction highlighted the diplomatic space created by Brics, which brings together countries with competing interests and positions on major geopolitical issues.
Modi-Xi-Putin-Pezeshkian project Brics unity
The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals involving PM Modi, Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, PM Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The visuals projected unity among members despite differences over conflicts and other major geopolitical issues.The interactions were particularly significant for India as it sought to use its Brics chairship to build consensus among countries with sharply different political and strategic priorities.Also read: PM doubles down on friendship with Iran, seeks win-win strategy; hope mounts for BRICS declaration
Gala dinner adds cultural dimension
Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner during the summit, providing an informal setting for interaction among heads of state and government.The specially curated Indian menu showcased regional flavours, traditional recipes and contemporary interpretations of Indian cuisine. The menu included Khandvi Mille-Feuille, Khumb Galouti, Paneer Lababdar, Gucchi Marmik, Carrot Bean Poriyal, Thakkali Belle Saaru, Millet Pulao, Beetroot Raita and assorted Indian breads.Desserts included Old Delhi Fruit Cream with Jalebi and Shahtoot Phirni.The cultural evening added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by negotiations over conflicts, terrorism, trade, energy and global governance.
Banyan tree plantation highlights sustainability
A symbolic Banyan tree plantation ceremony was also held during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the initiative.The Banyan tree, with its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness. The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".The plantation also reflected India's effort to connect the diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.
Brics Business Forum pushes trade, investment
The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders for discussions on trade, investment, finance, technology and development.PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying Brics countries account for 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and more than 25 per cent of global trade."The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date,” the Prime Minister said.Pezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing. Putin stressed that business-to-business ties and economic partnerships could help build more resilient international economic relations.
PM Modi pushes people-centric Brics
India's chairship sought to connect Brics cooperation more directly with ordinary citizens while focusing on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.Addressing the summit, PM Modi said, "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. India’s BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach."He said resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability had remained India's priorities, with special emphasis on connecting Brics cooperation with common people."Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."India organised more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements across around 30 cities during its 2026 chairship. The programme covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
Agriculture and healthcare get major push
Brics countries advanced cooperation in sustainable agriculture through Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology, a Digital Agriculture Network and the Brics AGRIN framework covering agricultural inputs, genetic resources and information.The Digital Agriculture Network is intended to expand the use of AI, geospatial technology, Internet of Things-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics to support farmers.In healthcare, the Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle and a roadmap for joint cooperation on healthy lifestyles were launched. Members also agreed to strengthen cooperation in traditional, complementary and integrative medicine.A greater focus was placed on mental health through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India serving as the coordinating centre.
Energy, climate and urban cooperation expanded
Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.The grouping also established a Brics Urban Mobility Hub to promote knowledge sharing and technical cooperation on sustainable urban transport. Members adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure and established an Urban Research and Knowledge Network.PM Modi also emphasised the importance of balancing development with environmental protection and said technology and critical minerals should not become instruments that hinder shared progress.
Startups, MSMEs and skilling receive boost
India advanced cooperation among small businesses and startups through a Brics MSME Cooperation Portal designed to connect MSMEs, financial institutions, technology centres, trade associations and policymakers.The Brics Incubator Network will connect startups and incubators across member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.The Brics Science and Research Repository was also welcomed as a platform for scientific knowledge sharing.Through Brics CONNECT, members also advanced cooperation on skills, employability, women's workforce participation, social security and digital public infrastructure.The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation, while sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a dedicated working group.
Supply chains and global value chains strengthened
Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.Members also gave in-principle approval to an agreement on cooperation and mutual administrative assistance in customs matters, aimed at facilitating trade, reducing transaction costs and improving border security and trade facilitation.
Global South gets stronger voice
PM Modi used the summit to push for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making institutions.He argued that the Global South should move from being a rule-taker to a rule-shaper and called for reforms in global governance, including greater representation in the UN Security Council.Brics also reaffirmed support for comprehensive UN reform and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.
New Delhi Declaration: 140 points, 45 pages
The Brics countries adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, a 45-page document containing 140 points, after intensive negotiations that continued into the early hours of Saturday.The declaration brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.Its adoption was particularly significant because the expanded Brics includes countries with differing positions on major geopolitical conflicts, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. India worked to bridge differences and secure consensus among members.
Pahalgam attack explicitly condemned
The declaration strongly condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and called for "zero tolerance for terrorism".It specifically condemned the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemned the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.The grouping also called for progress towards adopting the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.
West Asia: Restraint, ceasefire and diplomacy
The declaration expressed deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.It stressed dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and called for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.On Gaza, Brics called for upholding a ceasefire, ensuring unhindered humanitarian assistance and ending the forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.
Unilateral military action condemned
The declaration condemned unilateral military action without naming any country.The language assumes significance against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts in West Asia and the wider divisions within the expanded grouping.The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to reconcile competing positions and produce a common statement.
Trade, tariffs and sanctions
Brics expressed concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.The grouping reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and called for restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.Brics also voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter, calling for such measures to be eliminated.
Local currencies and financial resilience
The declaration backed efforts to promote cross-border payments and trade settlements using Brics members' local currencies while respecting national priorities.Members acknowledged work on the interoperability of payment and messaging systems and discussions on facilitating trade settlements and investment using local currencies.The push forms part of a broader effort to strengthen financial resilience and reduce vulnerabilities in international economic relations.
Critical minerals and energy security
The declaration stressed the importance of reliable, diversified, resilient and sustainable supply chains for critical minerals.It called for benefit sharing, value addition and economic diversification in resource-rich countries while recognising their sovereign rights over mineral resources.Brics also stressed the importance of critical minerals for zero and low-emission technologies, energy security and resilient energy supply chains.On energy, the declaration called for diversified sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets. It recognised that fossil fuels would continue to play an important role, particularly for emerging and developing economies, while backing equitable and inclusive energy transitions.
Health and universal health coverage
The declaration reaffirmed Brics' commitment to universal health coverage and resilient, inclusive and people-centred health systems.Members emphasised the coordinating role of the World Health Organisation and backed continued multilateral cooperation on global health.The declaration also covered the Pandemic Agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing negotiations, efforts to end tuberculosis, strengthening the health workforce, digital health and integration of traditional medicine.
Women, development and global governance
Brics recognised women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.The declaration stressed women's participation in governance and economic life, financial and digital inclusion, skill development, entrepreneurship and climate action.The grouping also reaffirmed the importance of reforming global institutions to reflect contemporary economic and political realities and strengthen the voice of developing countries.
The New Delhi Summit came as Brics entered its third decade with 11 full members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.India's 2026 chairship was its fourth after previous presidencies in 2012, 2016 and 2021. The latest chairship sought to build on those earlier efforts while adapting the grouping's agenda to its expanded membership.In his concluding remarks, PM Modi said the discussions had strengthened the view that Brics had evolved beyond a traditional grouping and could function as an ecosystem for practical solutions."Our discussions over the past two days have further strengthened our conviction that BRICS is not merely a grouping of nations, but an ecosystem of solutions. We hope that the New Delhi Declaration adopted at this summit will provide a clear direction for our shared vision and future cooperation. We must translate all outcomes into time-bound actions that deliver last-mile impact. We will work together to ensure that our framework moves beyond mere documentation and creates a tangible impact in real life," he said.PM Modi also said the world now expected concrete results from Brics rather than only ideas and commitments, as the grouping prepares to enter its third decade.
Ayush Pandey is a journalist at The Times of India, covering breaking news, politics, defence, and major legal and policy developments across India and the world. His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life.
He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. His work combines speed, clarity, and depth for a fast-moving digital audience.

articles.title: Poland warns of 'real' threat after Russian drones strike Ukraine near its border
articles.body:
Poland is treating Russian drone strikes near its border with Ukraine and the attack on a passenger train with the "utmost seriousness," Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said Sept. 13.
Russia launched drones overnight at western Ukraine, striking a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing and a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
Kierwinski confirmed that Russia first struck near the Dorohusk–Yahodyn border crossing and later hit the passenger train near the Polish border.
"We are treating these events with the utmost seriousness," Kierwinski wrote on X. "The situation is being constantly monitored. Russia is an enemy of the free world."
The overnight Russian drone assault brought the war unusually close to Poland's border, with multiple strikes reported in Volyn Oblast, Ukraine's northwest, near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk crossing.
Polish Armed Forces' Operational Command spokesperson Jacek Goryszewski said the threat to Poland was "real" as Russian forces attacked Ukrainian regions overnight.
"Drones were operating and even striking targets located very close to the Polish border — just a few to several dozen kilometers away," he said, according to Polish broadcaster RMF24.
The attacks also stranded Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna and members of an Estonian Foreign Ministry delegation at the border crossing. Tsahkna said they were unable to leave Ukraine because of the Russian drone threat.
"Russia's attacks are becoming more intense and moving ever closer to NATO and the EU. Our response must intensify, too," Tsahkna wrote on X. "Every Russian missile and drone Ukraine stops, every Russian capability we help Ukraine destroy, and every additional cost we impose on Moscow strengthens the security of Ukraine and all of Europe."
The overnight attack damaged a gas station near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk crossing in Volyn Oblast, Ukraine's northwesternmost region. Falling drone debris also sparked fires at the station and several trucks parked nearby, Volyn Customs spokesperson Valentyna Chernysh told Suspilne.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned the strike, warning that the attack brought Russia's war directly to the EU and NATO's doorstep.
"This is (Vladimir) Putin's terror, 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," Sybiha wrote on social media.
The Yahodyn border crossing itself was not hit and remains operational, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko told RBC-Ukraine.
Demchenko warned that Russian attacks in the area are intensifying and said the crossing could be temporarily closed if the security situation requires it.

articles.title: Ukraine has imposed sanctions on 20 vessels of russia’s shadow fleet, enterprises of the Rostec corporation, and propagandists
articles.body:
Ukraine has imposed sanctions on 20 vessels of russia’s shadow fleet, enterprises of the Rostec corporation, and propagandists
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy enacted sanctions against 20 vessels, 29 individuals, and 29 companies linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex and Rostec. The restrictions also targeted 10 propagandists.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed three decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine on imposing sanctions on vessels of Russia’s shadow fleet, against enterprises and individuals linked to the Russian state corporation "Rostec," and against propagandists who justify the aggression of the russian federation, UNN reports, citing the Office of the President.
Details
The sanctions list includes 20 seagoing vessels that Russia uses to export oil, petroleum products, and liquefied gas. This is the most important source of revenue for the Russian budget, directly financing the war against Ukraine. There is clear data proving that these tankers transport oil from Russian ports to India, Egypt, and Turkey. At the same time, they sail under the flags of Liberia, the Marshall Islands, Sierra Leone, Barbados, and Palau.
One of the decisions imposes sanctions on 29 citizens of the russian federation and 29 Russian companies. These include enterprises incorporated into supply chains for high-precision industrial equipment, electronics, and components used to manufacture missiles and drones. Restrictions have also been imposed on enterprises that produce dual-use goods, research organizations developing technical documentation for Russia’s military-industrial complex, as well as an educational institution that trains specialists for enterprises of the Russian Kalashnikov concern. Sanctions have also been imposed on companies that design solutions and supply high-tech equipment for enterprises of Russia’s military-industrial complex, as well as IT companies that develop and maintain software products for information encryption and database collection and management.
"Rostec" is the industrial core of Russia’s war machine: the corporation’s enterprises provide up to 80% of the weapons and military equipment used in the war against Ukraine and produce, in particular, Iskander and Kinzhal missiles, attack drones, and critical components for UAVs with which Russia attacks Ukraine," emphasized Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the adviser and Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy.
Another decision imposes restrictions on 10 Russian and Ukrainian individuals who spread disinformation and Russian propaganda and support Russia’s aggressive policy toward Ukraine. In particular, sanctions have been imposed on Yulia Mendel.
Ukraine will provide all the information to its partners to synchronize sanctions across international jurisdictions, the Office of the President concluded.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles hit Russian chemical plant
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant in Volgograd, Russia, with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles overnight on September 10-11, 2026.
- The U.S.-sanctioned facility produces combustion catalysts and other chemicals used in Russian aviation, shipbuilding and defense manufacturing.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a Russian chemical plant in Volgograd overnight on September 10-11, 2026, using FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missiles, according to Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that manufactures the weapon. Fire Point said the missiles hit their target directly and sparked a large fire at the facility.
The target, Volgogradpromproekt, is a specialty chemicals producer in Volgograd’s Kirovsky district. The company is under U.S. sanctions for supporting Russia’s military-industrial complex. It manufactures ferrocene-based combustion catalysts along with other chemicals, including organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants and resins, and Ukrainian monitoring groups say its products feed into Russian aviation, shipbuilding and defense manufacturing.
Ukrainian OSINT group Exilenova+ published satellite imagery it said showed one of the missiles had destroyed a roughly 20-by-15-meter section of the plant’s main production building. That damage estimate comes from the group’s own imagery analysis and has not been independently confirmed by other sources.
“Flamingos paid a little visit to Volgograd last night,” Fire Point said in a statement. “Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective.”
Russian officials offered a more limited account of the strike. Volgograd region Gov. Andrey Bocharov said only that debris from the attack had landed on the grounds of an industrial facility in the southern part of the city, a description that stops short of Fire Point’s claim of confirmed direct hits.
Defense analysts at Defence Express have suggested a reason Ukraine chose a large cruise missile over a cheaper drone for this particular target. The combustion catalysts Volgogradpromproekt produces are used in manufacturing solid rocket propellant, a component needed for missiles including Russia’s Iskander and Zircon systems. An FP-5, carrying roughly a metric ton of explosives, can do far more damage to a hardened industrial target than a drone strike, which may explain the choice of weapon for a plant that had not previously appeared on lists of well-known Russian defense contractors.
The FP-5 Flamingo is a ground-launched cruise missile that entered service in August 2025. Fire Point says it can carry a payload of up to 1,150 kg (2,535 lb) to targets as far as 3,000 km (1,860 miles) away, operating day or night and resisting electronic jamming.
The company describes it as the largest missile in its class while emphasizing that it remains relatively simple and inexpensive to build, with reusable launchers instead of costly dedicated launch platforms.
The strike on Volgogradpromproekt was one of several Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory reported the same night. Fire Point said its FP-1 drones separately struck an oil refinery and an Ozon logistics warehouse in Saratov, with the warehouse covering roughly 85,000 square meters and reportedly capable of storing more than 30 million items. A refinery in Volgograd was also targeted in a separate drone attack that night, according to local reports.

articles.title: Weekend of Russian airstrikes kills at least 10 across Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian airstrikes in several Ukrainian regions Saturday killed 10 people, injured dozens and damaged residential buildings and infrastructure, local officials said.
The civilian death toll rose sharply in Ukraine in the past two months as Russia stepped up attacks on power plants and other infrastructure. Ukraine hit energy facilities and warehouses in Russia and both sides targeted each other's shipping.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, writing on Telegram, said Russia deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since morning.
“The Russians expanded the war from the front, where they are unsuccessful, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war," Zelenskyy wrote.
“Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance,” Zelenskyy added.
The city council in Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine's frontline "fortress cities" that Russia wants to capture, said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people and injuring four in three incidents over a 90-minute period.
"These are not military targets," the council said. "They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business."
The governor of Ukraine's Zhytomyr region, west of Kyiv, Vitaliy Bunechko, said a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zvyahel.
Bunechko said two petrol stations also were attacked, as well as an unidentified "enterprise with foreign investment."
Earlier, Zelenskyy reported attacks on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, his hometown.
The governor of Zaporizhzhia region, Ivan Fedorov, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi Rih's military administration, said two people were killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles.
The Russian military said its forces hit Ukrainian steelmaker Zaporizhstal in Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro and several plants in Kryvyi Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex.
Reuters could not independently verify accounts from either side.
In the Black Sea port of Odesa, regional Gov. Oleh Kiper said nearly 40 people were injured in attacks that extended from overnight into Saturday evening.
The Russia-installed head of areas of eastern Donetsk region under Moscow's control said three people were killed in Ukrainian drone attacks.
In Moldova, on Ukraine's western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed.
Russian drones have regularly entered Moldovan airspace despite official protests. In one instance this week, the departure of Zelenskyy's aircraft to Norway was delayed.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Russia's forces maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, hitting a cargo ship in Odesa that it said was carrying goods for military use.
Earlier, the ministry said its forces struck two cargo vessels overnight in the port of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine's military said it hit one of Russia's largest synthetic rubber producers in Togliatti in the Samara region, causing a fire.
The Togliattikauchuk plant specialized in the production of synthetic rubbers and fuel additives used in fuel for Russian missiles, it said.
Russian regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said industrial facilities in the Samara region were attacked by Ukrainian drones, without specifying which facilities or whether they were damaged, Interfax news agency reported.
Ilya Sukhikh, mayor of Togliatti in the Samara region, said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis claim ballistic missile, drone attack on Saudi military base
articles.body:
Tarek Chouiref
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Yemen’s Houthi group said early Sunday that it had carried out an attack with ballistic missiles and drones on a military base in southern Saudi Arabia.
In a statement posted on US social media platform X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the attack targeted weapons depots and command-and-control rooms at the Sharurah base.
A large barrage of ballistic missiles and drones was used, he said, claiming the strikes hit their targets.
Saree said the attack was in response to continued Saudi attacks on Yemen. He warned of larger strikes deeper inside Saudi territory if they continue.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the Houthi claim.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense said earlier Saturday that a projectile landed in the Al-Tuwal governorate in the southwestern Jazan region, injuring two people.
It said the projectile also damaged a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles.
Yemen’s map of territorial control has changed in recent days amid escalating confrontations between government forces and the Houthis since July, following years of relative calm.
The Houthis now control the entire western Al-Hudaydah province, according to the group, after advancing in the western Taiz province and capturing the coastal city of Mokha and its Red Sea port.
Their advance also brought them close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime passageways.
Government forces, meanwhile, have made gains in the northern Al-Jawf province along the Saudi border and approached its provincial capital, Al-Hazm.
Clashes are also continuing on fronts in the Marib, Al-Bayda, and Al-Dhale provinces.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis captured the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014.
A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces announced advances in Al-Jawf province, which borders Saudi Arabia, and said they were approaching Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
 
Yemen had been under a relative lull since April 2022 after nearly 12 years of war between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and the Iranian-backed Houthis, who seized control of the capital, Sanaa, and large parts of the country in 2014.
Since late 2023, after the Gaza war began, the Houthis have become increasingly involved in regional hostilities, launching attacks on Israel and commercial shipping in the Red Sea, while recent renewed fighting has raised fears of a return to full-scale conflict in Yemen

articles.title: What are the five pros and cons of artificial intelligence?
articles.body:
What are the five pros and cons of artificial intelligence?
AI creates new opportunities in programming and automation, but experts warn of the spread of harmful content and risks to early-career workers.
Artificial intelligence has rapidly become a tool used by hundreds of millions of people, but tech leaders are sounding alarms against the rapid advancement of AI that is being seen as a threat to humanity.
AI systems can now generate text and images, write computer code, and perform complex analyses that once required a significant amount of time and human input.

- list 2 of 3Anthropic claims Claude AI used for missile projects, global espionage
- list 3 of 3Anthropic warns of bids to use AI to build biological weapons
Supporters argue these tools could raise productivity and create new kinds of work.
However, their rapid development has also raised concerns about job losses, the spread of misinformation, and the resources needed to power AI infrastructure. Researchers have also warned that regulation and safeguards are struggling to keep pace with the technology.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, whose company created AI tool Claude, said on Saturday. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”
So, what are the pros and cons of artificial intelligence, and where is this rapidly growing technology headed?
Boosts productivity and makes tasks easier
One of the obvious benefits of AI is its ability to help people complete some tasks more quickly.
AI tools are already being used for education, writing and editing text, gathering information, and computer programming.
Almost one billion people use AI for a wide range of tasks, according to the 2026 International AI Safety Report published by the United Kingdom’s government.
The report found that the most frequent queries by users on AI giant OpenAI’s ChatGPT platform involved practical guidance on editing or generating text, researching medical health, and searching for information.
There is also evidence of significant productivity gains in particular tasks. In September 2025, the Bank for International Settlements found generative AI had “productivity gains of between 10 and 65 percent, and efficiency gains of roughly 20 to 50 percent in time savings”.
Gains were particularly evident in industries such as “coding, consulting tasks and professional writing”, it added.
Indian technology company Wipro, for example, said its use of AI had freed up capacity equivalent to 20,000 employees, who were reassigned to other roles.
Creates new opportunities and skills
While AI is certainly bound to eliminate or transform some jobs, it is also spurring the creation of others.
Demand is increasing for skills that include machine-learning programming and chatbot development. Software developers are also increasingly using AI to produce code before checking and debugging the results.
The changes mean workers may increasingly need to learn how to use AI alongside traditional professional skills.
Wipro Chief Technology Officer Sandhya Arun said the company was training more than 100,000 employees in advanced AI skills as it shifts towards what it calls a “human-AI operating model”.
Threatens jobs
AI’s groundbreaking ability to automate work is also one of the biggest risks to society, experts say.
While no concrete data exists, some 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies and 40 percent in emerging economies could be vulnerable to AI, depending on how employers and workers adopt the technology, the 2026 International AI Safety Report warned.
Earlier this year, a slew of tech giants announced cuts amid growing reliance on and shifts towards AI.
Amazon slashed 16,000 jobs in a second wave of layoffs at the e-commerce giant in three months, while social media site Pinterest announced it would cut 780 jobs as the company reallocated resources amid increased investment in AI.
There are also concerns about people starting their careers.
Stephen Clare, lead writer of the 2026 International AI Safety Report, said there is “suggestive evidence” that early-career workers in occupations highly exposed to AI may be finding it harder to get jobs.
Can be misused and spread harmful content
Generative AI – which creates content based on existing data – can create convincing text, voices, images and videos, capabilities that can also be exploited.
AI-generated deepfakes have been used to scam people, and AI systems have also been used in cyberattacks.
Deepfake technology has been used to impersonate senior US officials and corporate executives.
Criminals can use synthetic voices and videos to make people reveal sensitive information, providing access to computer systems, and transferring money.
Uses significant energy and resources
AI technology depends on physical data centres filled with powerful computer chips, which require large amounts of electricity and cooling.
The expansion of data centres is raising questions about electricity supply and whether governments have enough infrastructure to support large AI projects.
For example, a proposed data centre in the US state of Utah would use more electricity than the entire state.
Beyond electricity, environmental activists in the United States are ringing the alarm over the enormous amounts of water needed to cool down servers at data centres at a time when parts of the country are experiencing droughts.
Some residents living near US data centres have also complained of the constant hum they emit. A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans oppose establishing AI data centres in their areas.
The concerns around data centres extend beyond just the US and the developed world.
In Kenya, a proposed $1bn data centre involving Microsoft and Emirati technology company G42 has drawn considerable attention.
Kenyan President William Ruto highlighted the scale of the centre’s energy demands, warning that the infrastructure of that size would require substantial additional power generation.

articles.title: AI giants call for slowdown over ‘serious’ risks
articles.body:
AI giants call for slowdown over ‘serious’ risks
OpenAI chief Sam Altman and xAI owner Elon Musk have backed calls to immediately slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models. Their statements came after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI could outpace human control and cause catastrophic damage within months.
Four days ago, researcher Jacob Coxon publicly resigned from Anthropic, accusing both the company and his previous employer, OpenAI, of racing towards self-improving super-intelligence without “acting responsibly.” He also claimed that the technology could “kill us all” by the end of the decade.
In a 3,800-word essay published on his personal website on Saturday, Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021, outlined “serious” dangers, including loss of control over AI systems, their misuse for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and major economic disruption. He said commercial competition could fuel a “race to the bottom” and exacerbate the threats.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote.
Altman agreed that the industry needed to “pace the frontier,” describing Anthropic’s proposal to give independent evaluators employee-like access to its systems as “a great idea.”
Musk, whose xAI is among the companies competing to develop increasingly advanced models, endorsed the call on X. “Dario is right,” he wrote, adding that he had been “sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.”
Amodei said the technology was advancing “drastically faster,” partly because of its growing ability to help build the next generation of models. Citing an incident in which OpenAI agents reportedly escaped a confined testing environment, he said that within six to 12 months a more capable swarm could “take over the entire internet” and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.
He proposed a three-step plan that he said could temper development without “sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States’ lead in AI.” The measures include giving outside evaluators deep access to developers’ systems, establishing common industry safety standards, and pursuing international coordination.
Anthropic was the first frontier AI company to deploy its technology on classified US government networks. Its Claude model was integrated into Palantir’s Maven system and reportedly helped generate, locate, and prioritize targets during the US bombing campaign against Iran. It was also reportedly used in the raid that captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
Anthropic later refused to lift safeguards against mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, arguing that current models remained too unreliable to make life-or-death decisions without human involvement.
The Pentagon insisted that providers must allow their technology to be used for “all lawful purposes” and subsequently designated Anthropic a national security supply chain risk. The company challenged the decision, with a California judge ruling in August that the department’s measures were “illegal and baseless,” although separate proceedings in Washington remain unresolved.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp has opposed calls to pause AI development, arguing that slowing progress would benefit US “adversaries.”

articles.title: Territory Remains Main Obstacle to Ukraine-Russia Deal, Kushner Says
articles.body:
Territorial disputes remain the central obstacle preventing Ukraine and Russia from reaching an agreement to end the war, US presidential special envoy Jared Kushner said on Sunday during the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) forum in Kyiv.
Addressing conference participants, Kushner explained that while mediators have assembled frameworks covering nearly all other facets of a prospective settlement, the division over front lines and sovereign borders has stalled diplomatic efforts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He stated that Russian President Vladimir Putin had detailed Moscow’s specific territorial objectives during recent Kremlin consultations, but Ukraine firmly refuses to make concessions or pull back its military forces.
“The main issue will be territories, and that is precisely where the sides have not yet reached an agreement,” Kushner said, as reported by Ukrinform.
“President Putin laid out his position regarding what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to retreat to that line, we would have already prepared and agreed on the remaining terms of the deal. Currently, Ukraine does not want to do this.
And our task as mediators is to figure out how we can find a creative solution that does not contradict their desires, helps them achieve their goals, and compels Russia to end the conflict so both sides can move forward within a framework that prevents a recurrence.”
Russia Fired 2,100 Drones and 78 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
Kushner did not address the widespread war crimes committed by Russian occupation forces or the legal question of Russian accountability for launching the full-scale invasion. Instead, he characterized both nations as enduring “a lot of pain” and asserted that both Kyiv and Moscow harbor a determination to bring fighting to an end.
“[US] President [Donald] Trump is very, very committed to this cause. Steve [Witkoff] and I are very committed. President Zelensky is very committed. From what we have seen and heard, President Putin is also very committed to this cause,” Kushner claimed. “It is simply a matter of finding the right formula that will hopefully satisfy everyone to move forward.”
Pre-winter ceasefire uncertainty and security guarantees
Asked whether a cessation of hostilities could be achieved before the onset of winter, Kushner gave a cautious response, acknowledging that diverse ideas have been floated by multiple actors without achieving a diplomatic breakthrough.
Kushner detailed that diplomatic discussions over recent months have concentrated extensively on future security architecture and security guarantees designed to assure Ukraine that any cessation of combat represents an enduring peace rather than an operational pause for Moscow to regroup.
He stressed that sovereignty, security, and economic prosperity form the three non-negotiable pillars of any just outcome for Ukraine.
Kushner revealed that during previous trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi, delegations from Ukraine, the US, and Russia finalized practical mechanisms for conflict prevention and ceasefire verification involving military personnel. He stated that this monitoring structure is engineered to take effect the moment political leadership resolves the territorial dispute.
“We have developed a monitoring mechanism that involves the military, and everyone agrees that once there is a definitive resolution regarding frontlines or territorial issues, a mechanism will exist that everyone can hopefully abide by,” Kushner explained.
“I think this is something that satisfies both sides, representing genuine progress in that regard.”
Post-war prosperity as an incentive for lasting peace
Outlining subsequent stages of the US diplomatic initiative, Kushner argued that long-term stability must be anchored in economic prosperity and mutual financial incentives.
He contended that both Ukraine and Russia should leverage a post-war settlement to attract international capital, create jobs, and raise living standards, suggesting that societal economic interest in stability serves as the most effective defense against renewed conflict.
“When you end a war, people must have something to look forward to,” Kushner said, asserting that President Trump shares this philosophy.
“Both countries need to consider how they can seize this opportunity after the war to attract investments, create employment, provide greater prosperity, and increase incomes. That is what motivates societies to invest in and feel enthusiastic about peace. In many ways, it becomes your greatest security guarantee. If everyone lives well and maintains a personal stake in security, it will hopefully produce something durable and sustainable.”
Kushner’s remarks arrive following multi-stage consultations held in Kyiv on Sept. 6 alongside fellow envoy Witkoff and European national security advisers, which succeeded a three-hour meeting with Putin in Moscow. During those talks, Putin insisted on achieving his stated war aims, with Kremlin insiders reiterating that Moscow will refuse any frontline ceasefire until Russian forces capture the entire Donbas.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior Ukrainian officials have categorically dismissed territorial concessions as unacceptable capitulation, maintaining that restoring territorial integrity and securing legally binding Western defense guarantees remain indispensable to any durable settlement.
