articles.title: Shadowy Iran security chief resurfaces to sabotage US deal, pushing war toward escalation
articles.body:
A secretive Iranian security hard-liner who returned to prominence after years in the shadows helped derail an attempt to reach an agreement with the United States, setting off one of the fiercest internal power struggles in Tehran since the war began, according to an extensive New York Times report.
The episode unfolded in July, shortly after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had completed negotiations on a memorandum of understanding to end the war with Washington. Pezeshkian traveled to neighboring Iraq for a week of mourning ceremonies for Iran’s former supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed at the beginning of the war.
Then came news that stunned him: Iranian forces had opened fire on three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, setting a Qatari liquefied natural gas tanker ablaze and damaging other ships.
According to five Iranian officials and two members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps cited by the Times, an enraged Pezeshkian called Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, the IRGC’s commander in chief, described the attacks as “reckless” and demanded answers.
Vahidi told the president that he had neither authorized the attack nor known about it beforehand. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council had also been unaware of the operation, according to the report.
Much of Iran’s leadership, it turned out, had no idea that a hard-line faction had decided to act on its own.
The covert maneuvering ultimately thwarted efforts by Iran’s relatively moderate faction to bring hostilities with the United States to an end. The hard-liners succeeded in part because the one person with the authority to settle such disputes — Iran’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei — has effectively become a ghost.
Pezeshkian immediately returned to Tehran. By the next morning, as the mourning ceremonies continued, the United States responded with airstrikes against Iran and fighting resumed.
Iranian officials and an IRGC member told the Times that what followed was one of the most heated political confrontations within Iran’s leadership. Senior officials engaged in shouting matches, two high-ranking generals threatened to resign and accusations of betrayal and treason flew between rival factions.
Officials said the fallout contributed to an upheaval at the Supreme National Security Council and a decision to put Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, a veteran politician and former IRGC commander, in charge of it. Rezaei was seen as having the political skills needed to mediate between the competing factions.
But the divisions have persisted and the hard-liners are now in an even stronger position.
The conflict has continued to escalate. Over the past week, Iran and the United States have again exchanged fire, with Iranian forces attacking U.S. Navy vessels for the first time and American forces destroying at least eight Iranian oil tankers.
A hard-liner returns from the shadows
Three Iranian officials said investigations by the government and security forces determined that the decision to attack the three commercial vessels in July had been made by Hossein Taeb, a powerful intelligence figure who had opposed the agreement with the United States from the outset.
According to the officials, Taeb told the new supreme leader that Iran had made a mistake by ending the war and agreeing to the deal.
In a recent speech to military families, Taeb said he was not opposed to talks in principle but drew a clear line over the terms.
“Negotiations that ignore the rights of our people and concede to the excessive demands of the enemy have no place in Iran’s politics,” he said.
Taeb, a shadowy cleric with deep roots in Iran’s security establishment, was recently appointed to lead the Basij, the paramilitary force used by the government to suppress domestic dissent.
He previously spent more than 20 years in senior intelligence positions, including as head of the IRGC’s intelligence organization, before Ali Khamenei removed him in 2022 after a series of security failures. Those included Israeli penetration of Iran’s security apparatus and the disruption of an Iranian plot in Turkey.
Taeb returned to prominence following Ali Khamenei’s killing. Officials said he played a central role in the selection of Khamenei’s son Mojtaba as his successor.
When Pezeshkian demanded to know who had ordered the attacks on the three vessels, he was told that commanders in the field had acted independently under an existing directive allowing them to attack any ship deemed to be violating Iran’s control over the strait without waiting for approval from central command.
One indication of the internal disagreement was that the IRGC’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters never claimed responsibility for the July 7 attack, even though it had routinely done so after attacks both before and after the incident.
Iranian officials provided the same explanation to the United States and several of its regional allies in the hours after the attacks, blaming “rogue” elements. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was dispatched to Oman, which has long served as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran, in an attempt to defuse tensions.
Where is Iran’s supreme leader?
The turmoil has renewed questions about Mojtaba Khamenei, whose whereabouts and role in governing Iran remain shrouded in secrecy.
This month, his mother-in-law, Tayebeh Mahrouzadeh, gave a lengthy video interview to a local journalist in which she described extraordinary security measures surrounding the family. She said relatives had no information about the whereabouts of the ayatollah or his three children.
Her husband, politician Gholam-Ali Haddad-Adel, told Iranian media in July that although Mojtaba Khamenei was not communicating with anyone because of security concerns, “God willing, he is healthy.”
Pezeshkian said in May that he had met Khamenei but did not say when or where.
Two Iranian officials and a former senior official described the circumstances of that encounter as highly unusual. They said Pezeshkian was transported in an ambulance with tinted windows while a secure video connection was established.
A man who said he was acting as an intermediary for Mojtaba appeared on a screen and purportedly relayed messages between the supreme leader and the president. Officials familiar with the encounter said Pezeshkian later told a close ally that he was not certain whether he had actually spoken with the supreme leader.
Last month, however, Pezeshkian said he had received permission for a second meeting and that it lasted seven hours.
“We talked about all the issues facing the country,” the president told Iranian state television, listing the cost of living, unemployment, sanctions, national unity and resilience during wartime.
He did not describe the circumstances of the meeting or disclose what Khamenei had said.
Tehran debates talks or a wider war
For weeks, according to the Times, the political leaders and generals running Iran have debated two competing strategies for breaking the deadlock with the United States.
Under one approach, Iran would attempt to return to negotiations. Under the other, it would dramatically escalate attacks against American targets, seeking to damage U.S. Navy vessels, kill American troops and drive up global oil prices.
Both strategies are aimed at ending the U.S. naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which has paralyzed trade and reduced Iranian oil sales to zero.
Hard-line generals, including Seyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force, have pushed for confrontation.
They told the Supreme National Security Council that they had developed a detailed war plan under which Iran and its regional allies — particularly the Houthis in Yemen and Iran-aligned militias in Iraq — would intensify attacks, including against oil facilities across the region.
The strategy would broaden the war and sharply increase its economic and military cost for the United States and its allies.
Pezeshkian and parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has been involved in negotiations with Washington, were among those warning that such a strategy could drag Iran into an abyss, risking even more devastating U.S. airstrikes and further crippling economic pressure.
For now, however, the hard-line faction appears to have prevailed.
“The war between Iran and the United States has entered the phase of escalation,” Mahdi Mohammadi, the top adviser to Ghalibaf, told the Times.

articles.title: Russian drone hits passenger train headed from Kyiv to Warsaw
articles.body:
Russian drone hits passenger train headed from Kyiv to Warsaw
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded to the attack by stating that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces are “knocking directly on the doors of the EU and NATO.”
Ukraine's Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces are “knocking directly on the doors of the EU and NATO.” | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Russian drones attacked a crossing point on the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday morning, hitting a passenger train two kilometers from the frontier in Volyn Oblast.
Ukraine’s state rail operator confirmed that a strike hit the locomotive of a passenger train bound for Warsaw. The train crew were warned of the threat in advance by Ukrainian authorities and no one was injured, the operator added.
Separately, social media videos showed a large fire at a gas station near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk crossing point between Ukraine and Poland. According to local media, there are no reports yet of casualties from the gas station fire.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded to the border strikes with a post on X stating that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces are “knocking directly on the doors of the EU and NATO.”
“Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” Sybiha added, urging Ukraine’s allies to “throw the full weight of your sanctions at Putin’s aggressive regime.”
Attacks on the EU’s borders have intensified as some intelligence agencies warn of a buildup towards a direct attack by Russia on a NATO member country. Europe faces “an escalating campaign of threats” and “hybrid warfare,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last month.

In July 2024, two H-6s were spotted conducting joint patrol near Alaska for the first time with their Russian counterpart, the Tu-95, prompting the US-Canadian North American Aerospace Defence Command to scramble their fighter jets.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Injure 23 Across Odesa, Ternopil, and Konotop
articles.body:
Russian forces launched widespread missile and drone strikes across Ukraine on Sunday morning, Sept. 13, hitting residential areas, civilian facilities, and transport infrastructure in Odesa, Ternopil, and Konotop, leaving at least 23 people injured.
In the southern port city of Odesa, a continuous combined missile and drone assault caused extensive damage across multiple municipal districts and injured at least nine civilians, according to Odesa City Military Administration Head Serhiy Lysak.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Already five casualties are known as a result of the enemy’s massive attack on Odesa,” Lysak stated on Telegram, adding that residential areas sustained heavy structural damage as emergency responders worked across affected sites.
Odesa Regional Military Administration Head Oleh Kiper reported that the morning bombardment struck both residential high-rises and private properties, while also damaging cultural and healthcare facilities.
“A continuous mass missile and drone attack by the enemy is ongoing. Russian forces are striking civilian infrastructure across Odesa region,” Kiper said.
“The morning attack damaged the upper floors of a multi-story apartment building and private residences. A fire also broke out on the territory of the Botanical Garden. Warehouses and a children’s sanatorium sustained damage.”
Kiper warned residents that the aerial threat remained active, urging civilians to remain inside shelters until all-clear signals were sounded.
Russian Strikes Hit Gas Station, Kyiv-Warsaw Train, Near Polish Border
Later, the number of casualties from the Russian attack on Odesa rose to 20, including two children.
“Twenty people have already been injured as a result of the enemy attack on Odesa. Among them are two children: a boy born in 2010 and a girl born in 2017,” Lysak said.
Drone strikes hit transport and industrial infrastructure in Ternopil
In western Ukraine, Russian attack drones targeted the regional center of Ternopil, striking transport and industrial facilities and injuring one person, municipal and regional officials reported.
Ternopil Mayor Serhiy Nadal confirmed an impact on urban infrastructure, noting that emergency crews from the State Emergency Service (SES) deployed to contain the aftermath.
Ternopil Regional Military Administration Head Taras Pastukh reported that Ukrainian air defense units intercepted the majority of incoming aerial munitions, though falling debris and impacts caused localized damage.
“A transport infrastructure facility and an industrial building were hit,” Pastukh said. “SES rescue teams are working on site, and the fire has been extinguished.”
Residential strike in Konotop, Sumy region
In northeastern Ukraine, Russian strike drones attacked the city of Konotop in the Sumy region on Sunday morning, injuring two civilians, according to the State Emergency Service.
The SES Main Directorate in Sumy region reported that the drone strike damaged a private residential dwelling and ignited a blaze that consumed an adjacent garage and a parked passenger automobile.
Firefighting crews extinguished the fire, while medical personnel provided emergency treatment to an injured man and woman at the scene.
Consecutive weekend assaults on southern Ukraine
The Sunday morning bombardments follow consecutive Russian strikes across southern Ukraine late Saturday, Sept. 12, and overnight into Sunday, Sept. 13.
In Odesa, an earlier strike around midnight damaged a multi-story residential building, following an alert issued by the Ukrainian Air Force tracking incoming Russian “Banderol” loitering munitions.
Earlier on Saturday evening, a Russian jet-powered drone hit a distribution depot belonging to postal and logistics company Nova Poshta in the Odesa region, wounding two people and damaging the facility’s facade, glazing, and freight vehicles.
Concurrently on Saturday evening, Russian forces struck electrical power infrastructure in neighboring Mykolaiv, causing widespread localized blackouts across multiple city districts before repair crews were dispatched to restore municipal power supplies.

articles.title: UAE and Iran leaders meet at the BRICS summit for the first time since the war
articles.body:
The talks follow the UAE’s suspension of trade and financial dealings with Iran in August and follow UAE's firm position that trust with Iran "is a mountain to climb" after Iran's attacks on the Gulf countries.
Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan met Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday during the BRICS summit in India, weeks after the UAE announced a suspension of trade and financial dealings with Tehran.
The talks mark the countries’ highest-level meeting since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, as the UAE has been making it clear through presidential diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash that "trust is the mountain we will have to climb," as "geography leaves us no alternative to engagement," but that those relations will need to be judged by actions and not words to rebuild the shattered trust.
The Abu Dhabi Media Office said the two leaders stressed the importance of supporting efforts to reduce tensions and strengthen regional stability.
On 19 August, the UAE’s foreign ministry announced that it had halted all trade and financial transactions with Iran until further notice, citing regional escalation.
The same statement reaffirmed the UAE’s commitment to dialogue and regional cooperation. Saturday’s account of the meeting did not announce a change to the trade restrictions or a specific agreement between the two countries.
Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz explained in a post on X that "despite all the bad blood between Abu Dhabi and Tehran, the emerging Gulf approach, and particularly the UAE’s, is increasingly clear: manage the Iranian risk rather than push Tehran into a corner."
"This does not mean trust. Rebuilding even a basic level of confidence between the two sides will take years. But from Abu Dhabi’s perspective, maintaining channels with Tehran is itself a form of strategic hedging. The UAE has little interest in becoming a frontline state in another regional war," the Israeli security analyst said.
Calls to protect trade and energy
Both countries are members of BRICS, the group of emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.
They backed the summit’s New Delhi Declaration, adopted on Saturday, which expressed concern over escalating tensions in the Middle East and called for “maximum restraint”.
The declaration urged the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect for national sovereignty and a lasting settlement through diplomacy. Leaders also called for cooperation to keep global trade, supply chains and energy moving, in line with international law.
Chinese President Xi Jinping urged BRICS to help bring peace to the region, saying China would work with other members towards that goal.
The declaration also criticised unilateral tariffs and sanctions and supported further work on international payments and trade using members’ own currencies.
Speaking on Sunday at the BRICS Plus outreach session, which brings members together with other invited countries, Pezeshkian said attacks on a country’s economic and energy infrastructure had consequences beyond its borders.
He said unilateral sanctions affected food security and people’s welfare, and called for greater use of national currencies and a stronger role for the New Development Bank, the lender established by BRICS countries.
Hormuz talks planned in Oman
Separately, Pezeshkian said Arab foreign ministers were due to meet in Muscat on Monday to sign an agreement establishing a joint Iran-Oman shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, disregarding the Gulf countries' united position that the strait must be open to free international navigation.
The UAE president's diplomatic advisor Anwar Gargash underlined days ago the country's firm position that it would not accept a single state's control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and that it was unacceptable for oil tankers to be threatened and attacked while attempting to transit the key waterway.
“Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity,” Gargash said.
In an interview published on Saturday, Pezeshkian said the International Maritime Organisation would then be informed of the agreement.
Iran had already announced on 5 August that it had agreed the location of a proposed shipping route with Oman.
At the time, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the arrangement alone could not guarantee safe navigation while the US naval blockade and other actions against Iran continued.
Pezeshkian also said in Saturday’s interview that Iran would reopen the strait when the United States ended its blockade and attacks. His remarks did not set a date for reopening the waterway.
On Sunday, Qeshm governor Amir Teymouri said one person had been killed after a merchant vessel was struck near Iran's Hengam and Qeshm islands. He did not identify the source of the strike.

articles.title: With U.S. diesel above $6 a gallon, Trump urges Ukraine to stop targeting Russian production facilities
articles.body:
With U.S. diesel above $6 a gallon, Trump urges Ukraine to stop targeting Russian production facilities
U.S. President Donald Trump said he had urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop striking Russian facilities that produce diesel fuel.
“We spoke to Mr. Zelensky about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel. That’s hurting the world,” Trump told reporters at a golf tournament in Ireland, according to Reuters.
Trump said strikes on Russian oil refineries were causing diesel shortages and driving up prices. The global shortage “isn’t done by the Middle East, this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” he said.
According to Reuters, the price of a gallon of diesel in the United States has risen above $6 for the first time. A gallon is about 3.8 liters. Diesel prices matter in part because trucks and agricultural machinery run on the fuel, so higher prices raise the cost of consumer goods.
According to Reuters, rising global oil prices are the main reason fuel prices have increased. In recent days, North Sea Brent crude has risen to $107.60 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude has climbed to $102.50 a barrel. Global oil prices are rising because of the ongoing U.S. and Israeli war with Iran.

articles.title: Senior Western figures at Ukraine station before Russia train strike, rail operator says
articles.body:
Senior Western figures at Ukraine station before Russia train strike, rail operator says
Former UK PM Boris Johnson and ex-CIA director David Petraeus were at Yagodyn station just before Russia attacked a Kyiv to Warsaw train
Ukraine’s state railway operator said top Western figures – including former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and ex-CIA director David Petraeus – were at a west Ukrainian railway station just before Russia struck a Warsaw-bound train there.
“Shortly before the locomotive was hit at the Ukrainian-Polish border, a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station,” Ukraine’s rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in a statement.
“There were, among others, security advisers from several EU member states and former European leaders on board, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson. In another train that was at Yagodyn station at the very moment of the attack was former CIA Director David Petraeus.”
“Putin escalates,” Poland’s Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote on social media. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a crisis team for the afternoon. Western politicians travelling to Kyiv rely on the rail link from Poland to Ukraine as the country’s airspace is closed.
Passengers were evacuated in time and nobody was harmed, Ukrainian Railways said on Sunday.
Polish railway operator PKP said it had taken over the train from the Ukrainian side with a delay of more than six hours and it was continuing on to Warsaw.
Poland’s Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said a drone also struck in western Ukraine 1km (0.6 miles) from Poland’s border and another at a distance of 5km. Polish F-16 fighter jets and a reconnaissance aircraft monitored the situation, he said. Polish airspace was not violated.

articles.title: Russia launches more than 450 drones in overnight attacks while Ukraine strikes oil refineries
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during an interview on Saturday that he was willing to travel to the G20 summit in Miami to meet on the sidelines with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Russia launched over 450 drones across Ukraine in overnight attacks, according to Ukraine's Armed Forces, while Kyiv struck oil refineries in Russia's Tatarstan, according to Russian authorities.
Russia launched 453 drones of various types across Ukraine, 409 of which were neutralised by Ukraine's Armed Forces. However, 13 locations were struck.
Multiple attacks on the city of Stryi, in the Lviv region, which borders Poland, left a multi-storey residential building, an outbuilding near a school and buildings near a railway station damaged after being struck by Russian drones.
In the city of Izyum, a 26-year-old woman died as a result of the detonation of an explosive device, according to the Head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, Oleh Syniehub, while the city of Kharkiv and 15 settlements in the Kharkiv region were subjected to Russian attacks, leaving three people injured, including a 73-year-old woman, Syniehub added.
On Saturday, at least five people were injured in the region of Volyn in western Ukraine after Russian forces launched a mass attack which lasted more than four hours, according to the regional Governor Roman Romaniuk, with more than 10 drones flying in the region's airspace.
One train in Lutsk which had been evacuated was struck by debris, sparking a fire. No injuries were reported, according to the governor.
Ukraine strikes oil facilities
Meanwhile, two people were killed and 12 were injured following a Ukrainian drone attack which sparked a fire at an industrial facility in Nizhnekamsk, Russia's Republic of Tatarstan, home to a major oil refining and petrochemical hub, according to Russian authorities.
Ukraine Defence Intelligence also said it had struck the Slavyansk-ECO oil refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Russia's southeastern region of Krasnodar Krai, hitting a key oil-processing unit and the refinery's tank farm.
Russia and Ukraine continue to target each other's energy-related facilities ahead of the winter. While Russia has focused on Ukraine's electricity and energy, Ukraine has mainly targeted Russia's oil and gas infrastructure.
Russia says Putin meeting with Zelenskyy at G20 'impossible'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during an interview on Saturday that he was willing to travel to the G20 summit in Miami to meet on the sidelines with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions," adding, "It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter. Results matter. That's it."
But Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov called that option "impossible" and said that Putin will only meet with Zelenskyy in Moscow.
Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Russia will not cease its "special military operations" in Ukraine during possible peace talks.

articles.title: Three years before 9/11, CIA warned Clinton that Bin Laden wanted to strike India
articles.body:
Three years before the 9/11 attacks shocked the United States, then-President Bill Clinton was warned by the CIA that Osama bin Laden intended to carry out attacks in India, Pakistan, Uganda and possibly Nigeria.A newly declassified CIA warning dated August 28, 1998, said Bin Laden had survived US missile strikes in Afghanistan and retained a network of individuals and allied groups across at least 60 countries that could be used to mount attacks.The assessment specifically listed India and Pakistan, along with Egypt, the Arabian Peninsula – particularly Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Yemen – Uganda and possibly Nigeria, as countries where Bin Laden intended to conduct attacks.
Bin Laden also viewed India as part of what he described as a “Crusader-Zionist-Hindu” conspiracy against the Islamic world, reflecting the ideological lens through which he framed India and its relationship with the US and Israel.The CIA said Bin Laden was also considering further attacks against the US and UK, although he had not indicated precise targets or timing.
The assessment came weeks after the August 1998 bombings of US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, which killed more than 200 people and brought Bin Laden's organisation firmly into the sights of US counterterrorism agencies.
The newly released document said Bin Laden’s infrastructure in North America, Europe and East Asia also lent credibility to reports that he could target US interests in those regions.The CIA assessment further noted that Bin Laden had authorised an associate to explore attacks in the US and that US officials had recently helped arrest Bin Laden operatives preparing attacks in Tirana and possibly Baku.
The India reference is significant because it shows that the threat posed by Bin Laden’s network was being assessed as extending beyond the Middle East, Africa and the US well before the September 11 attacks.The August 1998 assessment was part of a series of intelligence warnings about Bin Laden that accumulated in the years before 9/11. The newly released material includes warnings about his pursuit of unconventional weapons, potential attacks on US soil and, later, the possibility of aircraft hijackings.The documents also show that Bin Laden’s network was not viewed as a purely Afghanistan-based threat. The CIA described a global infrastructure capable of supporting or inspiring attacks across multiple regions.For India, the 1998 assessment offers an early glimpse of how New Delhi had already figured in US intelligence assessments of the emerging Bin Laden threat, years before the attacks that would transform global counterterrorism policy.
Prisha Patnaik is a journalist with The Times of India, writing across geopolitics, international affairs, culture, history and internet culture. With over two years of experience in social media and digital content, she is interested in how news, politics and culture are shaped for digital audiences. She holds a master’s degree in Media and Communications from Goldsmiths, University of London.

articles.title: The new strategic power of the Resistance
articles.body:
The new strategic power of the Resistance
Kayhan, in a note discussing recent developments in the Middle East, argues that a new strategic power structure has emerged within the Resistance axis. This new power is the result of several interconnected factors: Iran’s ability to overcome and outmaneuver the United States, Israel, and their regional allies, Yemen’s offensive military capabilities, and the steadfastness of Lebanon and Palestine.
These elements have combined to create a coherent and consolidated strategic force that has “broken through all barriers” and established a new regional equation stretching from the Mediterranean Sea to the Indian Ocean. This new equation has taken shape over nearly three decades of conflict, and despite the severity of ongoing events, it is now entering a phase of final stabilization. When, in the midst of Yemen’s successful operations and Iran’s repeated strikes, certain Arab governments ask Iran to reduce tensions with the United States, Israel, and themselves, it reveals that all previous options against the Resistance have become obsolete. The current moment is one of consolidating the Resistance’s major achievements, and that such consolidation requires a cleansing of the region, meaning the removal of destabilizing or hostile elements.
Sobh-e-No: BRICS; from potential cooperation to operational implementation
Sobh-e-No analyzed President Pezeshkian’s trip to New Delhi for the BRICS summit. The visit has two main dimensions. First, bilateral relations between Iran and India. The meeting between Pezeshkian and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted the importance of Tehran–New Delhi ties. Both sides emphasized expanding cooperation and continuing strategic agreements. Second, turning BRICS cooperation into practical mechanisms. Tehran’s focus during this trip was on ensuring that BRICS membership does not remain at the level of political dialogue. Instead, Iran wants BRICS capacities to be transformed into operational frameworks in areas such as trade, financial systems, use of national currencies, and broader economic cooperation. The simultaneous presence of both leaders at the BRICS summit created an opportunity to pursue bilateral and multilateral diplomacy at the same time.
Javan: The Strait of Hormuz will not be reopened
Javan discussed the recent understanding reached between Tehran and Muscat, with Persian Gulf foreign ministers present. According to the paper, the agreement is strictly technical, concerning the details of new entry and exit routes in the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman. Other Persian Gulf states are attending the meeting only to signal their implicit non‑objection to the international community. Javan emphasizes that this understanding does not mean the Strait of Hormuz will reopen. Iran has delivered seven conditions to the United States through intermediaries. These conditions have been approved by Iran’s highest authorities, and until they are fully implemented, the strait will remain closed. Thus, the Iran–Oman agreement does not signify reopening; rather, it establishes that if the strait is eventually reopened, it will be done under this specific framework, which the paper describes as a major step in asserting Iran’s sovereignty. Any reopening depends entirely on US compliance with Iran’s conditions.
Ham‑Mihan: Why has Iran’s nuclear file returned to the UN Security Council?
Ham‑Mihan explains that Western governments are trying to move Iran’s nuclear issue from the IAEA Board of Governors back to the UN Security Council to create a “two‑track process.” Track One is the JCPOA & Snapback Mechanism. This track is based on alleged Iranian violations of the JCPOA. However, China and Russia opposed this path in the Security Council, preventing it from gaining full legal legitimacy. Track Two is Safeguards Non‑Compliance Referral. This new track focuses on alleged Iranian non‑compliance with its IAEA safeguards agreement. The key difference of the second track is that because in the Board of Governors, there is no veto, so a resolution can be passed and the case referred to the Security Council. Once referred, China and Russia cannot easily dismiss the IAEA’s findings and will face a more difficult diplomatic position. Ham‑Mihan argues that the Western goal is for these two tracks to reinforce each other, increasing pressure on Iran.
Farhikhtegan: Dynamite in the oil market
Farhikhtegan analyzed the reasons behind the surge in oil prices above $100 per barrel. The paper says that although analysts cite various factors, they all agree on one central issue: geopolitical developments in Yemen and around the Bab al‑Mandab Strait. Energy experts argue that the main issue is not just reduced supply but the shrinking security margin of the global oil market. Key factors include: ongoing restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz, increased control by Yemen’s Ansarallah around Bab al‑Mandab, reduced Russian supply and refining capacity, declining global inventories, and changes in China’s oil purchasing patterns. However, the $109 price recorded on Thursday night was clearly the result of Ansarallah’s dramatic and rapid territorial advances, which sharply intensified geopolitical risk and pushed prices beyond the $100 threshold.

articles.title: Russia hits truck near Polish border in latest strike near NATO
articles.body:
Russia attacked a truck near Ukraine's border with Poland, Polish and Ukrainian officials said on Sunday, the latest strike to hit areas near NATO as Moscow and Kyiv intensify their long-distance strikes to try to shift momentum in the war.
Polish border guards told Reuters that the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack around 800 meters (half a mile) from Poland, but that the crossing has since resumed operations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in Western Ukraine. Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.
Russia has begun targeting Ukraine's border crossings with its Western allies in recent weeks, part of a growing campaign by both sides to erode the other's economic infrastructure more than four years into Russia's invasion.
India, China offer to broker peace talks
In India, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had been attending the BRICS summit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had offered help brokering a peace settlement, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Last month, at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Modi told Putin that the war must end, one of several calls for peace by leaders of nations that have traditionally strong relations with Russia.
Last month, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly told Putin that he should halt the conflict along the front line, which has remained largely static this year.
Russia has ruled that out, saying Ukraine should pull back to leave the industrialized eastern Donbas region in Moscow's hands, something Kyiv has said it will never do.
Both Brazil and China, themselves founding BRICS members, have called for a resumption of peace talks.
TASS cited Peskov as saying that Putin had informed Modi of the situation "on the ground" in Ukraine, and that Russia had not ruled out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October.
Trump tells Ukraine's Zelenskiy to stop hitting Russian diesel
US President Donald Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure.
"We spoke to Mr. Zelenskiy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel," Trump told journalists during a visit to Ireland.
"You have to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," he said.

articles.title: Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
articles.body:
- Category

Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
A Russian-linked hacking operation used Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence models to automate cyberespionage targeting Ukrainian government officials, military personnel, diplomats, defense companies, and drone technology suppliers, with more than 20 organizations identified as targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a threat intelligence report published by Anthropic on September 10, the company tracked the group as GTG-20006 and said its attribution was consistent with public reporting linking the activity to Midnight Blizzard, a Russian state-linked hacking group.
Anthropic said the hackers used customized AI-driven workflows to automate much of the attack process, including reconnaissance, acquiring infrastructure, phishing, maintaining access to compromised systems, and extracting stolen information.
The company identified more than 20 organizations targeted during planning, reconnaissance, or active operations. They included government ministries, intelligence and defense agencies, diplomatic missions, think tanks, and defense companies, primarily in Ukraine and Europe.
Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic personnel were among the most frequent targets. The group scanned email and remote-access systems belonging to more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations, according to Anthropic.
Drone technology was another major focus. The hackers exported mailboxes belonging to at least two drone component manufacturers, targeted a military drone producer, and stole a proprietary software development kit used for a drone vision system.
Anthropic said the attackers spent several days reverse-engineering the stolen software, reconstructing the system’s architecture, hardware components, supplier dependencies, and details of an unreleased product. Firmware related to military drone control and AI-based vision systems appeared to be of particular interest.
Claude was also incorporated into malware development and evasion. Anthropic found that AI agents monitored whether security software detected the group’s malicious programs. When a tool was flagged, the system could identify the affected component, modify it, rebuild the malware, and repeat the process until existing security products no longer detected it.
The hackers also used AI to research and register domains, configure phishing infrastructure, send malicious emails, monitor successful compromises, harvest credentials, and move through victims’ networks.
According to Anthropic, Claude assisted with processing and organizing hundreds of gigabytes of stolen information, including bulk exports from compromised email accounts. The AI was also used to help preserve access to infiltrated systems and automatically register attacker-controlled devices inside compromised organizations.
The operation sometimes targeted organizations connected to intended victims rather than attacking them directly. Anthropic said the hackers compromised at least three companies providing hotel guest Wi-Fi services and changed DNS records to redirect connected devices toward infrastructure controlled by the attackers.
The technique allowed the group to collect information about hotel guests and deliver malware to Windows, Android, and iOS devices. Individuals connected to Ukraine, including government officials and drone manufacturers, were among the targets.
The hackers also targeted WhatsApp accounts by linking attacker-controlled devices to victims’ profiles. Using automation tools, they suppressed read receipts while exporting conversations in Ukrainian and Russian. Anthropic said at least two former senior Ukrainian officials were targeted through the method.
In another part of the operation, the group exploited authorization weaknesses in video surveillance services to obtain tokens providing access to victims’ live camera feeds.
The same actor was linked by Anthropic to an intrusion into a North African government technology agency, where hackers stole a database containing more than 300,000 national identity records and commercial registry information covering more than half a million companies.
Russian-linked hackers have also been tied to major cyberattacks against Western companies. In June, The New York Times reported that Russian hackers were behind the 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover, which halted production for five weeks and caused an estimated $2.5 billion in damage to the UK economy.

articles.title: Sikorski Urges Aggressive NATO Drills Near Kaliningrad
articles.body:
NATO should conduct aggressive military exercises along the borders of Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave to exploit Moscow’s local troop drawdown and compel the Kremlin to divert forces away from Ukraine, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said on Friday, Sept. 11.
Speaking at the 22nd Annual Meeting of the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) in Kyiv, organized by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation, Sikorski stated that Poland monitors the Russian exclave closely and observed that Moscow has left the heavily militarized territory virtually depleted of conventional ground forces to replenish combat losses in Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Putin knows, or assumes, that NATO is a peaceful alliance and we will not take advantage of his local weakness. And, perhaps, that is a mistake,” Sikorski told conference participants, as reported by European Pravda.
Clarifying that he was not advocating for allied forces to seize the Baltic enclave, Sikorski emphasized that NATO should use high-intensity maneuvers to inject strategic unpredictability into Moscow’s defense planning.
“I propose that we hold drills on our side so aggressive that he is not sure what exactly we will do,” Sikorski explained. “And so that because of this, he would be forced to redeploy part of his forces from Ukraine.”
Heightened border alert
Sikorski’s remarks follow warnings from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk that Moscow may orchestrate provocations and strikes targeting border infrastructure between Ukraine and neighboring allied nations.
Territory Remains Main Obstacle to Ukraine-Russia Deal, Kushner Says
Speaking in Bratislava on Sept. 10, Tusk announced that Polish security services had cooperated with Ukrainian counterparts overnight to avert a direct threat to a border checkpoint.
Tusk noted that Russian forces had already targeted border transit hubs, pointing to a deadly drone strike on the Tudora-Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Sept. 8-9 that killed two Ukrainian nationals and injured seven others.
Tusk stated that he had reviewed intelligence dispatches received directly from the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) detailing anticipated Russian escalations in the coming months, urging European allies to reinforce collective defenses across NATO’s eastern flank.
Concurrently, Poland’s Minister Coordinator of Special Services Tomasz Siemoniak met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe in Washington to assess the threat of Russian hybrid warfare and conventional aggression against alliance members.
Ratcliffe’s prior diplomatic discussions in Moscow reportedly included direct warnings cautioning the Kremlin against testing allied commitments in the Baltic region.

articles.title: 'Immoral and self-destructive' — Zelensky blasts EU for considering lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs
articles.body:
'Immoral and self-destructive' — Zelensky blasts EU for considering lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs
President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized the European Union for so far failing to reach an agreement to extend sanctions against Russian oligarchs and businesses, calling it "immoral and self-destructive" in remarks on Sept. 12.
The EU has until Sept. 15 to renew its sanctions on more than 3,000 primarily Russian entities and individuals, but failed again on Sept. 11 to approve the extension. The measures were last extended on March 14.
Slovakia is holding up the agreement by repeating its call to lift sanctions against Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov — and for the first time, France has joined Bratislava in pushing for Usmanov to be delisted, four EU diplomats told the outlet Euronews.
Zelensky called out Fridman and Usmanov by name in a social media post on Sept. 12, demanding that the EU mount pressure against Russia's business sector rather than easing sanctions.
"When the Ukrainian economy is simply a target for Russia, it is certainly not the time for Europe to view Russian oligarchs as friends," he said.
"When Russia uses every euro and dollar to prolong the war, it is immoral and self-destructive to give Russian businesses the opportunity to live in a way that allows them to avoid the consequences of the war. Usmanov and Fridman represent the very type of Russian business that needs to find the courage to take concrete steps against the war."
read also
Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group and a member of Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Investigative reporters revealed in May 2023 that subsidiary Alfa Insurance provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine. The company has also reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
Usmanov is a Russian-Uzbek businessman who made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
Slovakia, arguably the most Kremlin-friendly government in the EU, has long called for the bloc to remove both Fridman and Usmanov from its sanctions list. France joining the demand is new, and has caused "huge frustration" among member states, diplomats told Euronews.
France reportedly is presenting the delisting of Usmanov as a political compromise, believing Slovakia is unlikely to give up both its demands in order to reach an agreement.
Extending the EU sanctions requires a unanimous vote, meaning one member state has veto power over the renewal.
read also
However, there is little risk that the sanctions will lapse, an EU diplomat told the Kyiv Independent. The worst-case scenario would likely mean the measures would only be extended six months (instead of the desired 12), rather than expire altogether.
Ambassadors will convene again on Sept. 14, with the aim of reaching an agreement by the 15th.
Zelensky urged the EU to consider Russia's escalating assault against Ukraine's economy when finalizing its sanctions list. He emphasized that Russia continued to launch large-scale drone attacks, aiming to "destroy the Ukrainian economy in ordr to break our resistance."
"Russian businesses that pay taxes into the war budget, and Russian oligarchs ... must feel that there is no safe place for them in the world as long as this war continues," he said.
The president did not single out France or Slovakia in his comments, but made it clear he did not support lifting sanctions against the Kremlin's billionaires — especially on a day of mass drone strikes across Ukraine.
"Five hundred Shahed drones per day is certainly not the right time to even begin a discussion about easing sanctions," he said.

articles.title: The Guardian view on Russian parliamentary elections: glimpses of weakness behind the facade | Editorial
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin’s authoritarian powers are not constrained by elections, but he is alert to the danger that his rule would look illegitimate without them. That creates a tension, which is resolved through “managed democracy” – a euphemism for fraud and repression camouflaged with ritual ballots, held under a constitution that notionally guarantees political freedoms but in reality serves only the president.
Russians are invited to elect a new Duma, the lower chamber of parliament, later this week, but they know in advance that United Russia, the official party of Putinism, will win a majority.
Engineering that outcome is not without risk for the ruling regime. The mechanics of stealing an election are simple enough. Ballots can be stuffed, official media are pliant. But too blatant a theft can be counterproductive. If the results are wildly divergent from most people’s sense of the real public mood, an authoritarian leader risks advertising his fear of a genuine democratic consultation. It is a sign of weakness.
To an extent, this has happened already. Last month, the supreme court blocked Yabloko, an old and marginal liberal party, from appearing on Duma ballot papers. The case was spurious to the point of absurdity.
Yabloko is not one of the pseudo-opposition “system” parties that provide a pretence of pluralism in parliament, but nor does it pose a serious challenge to the regime. If it did, it wouldn’t have survived this long. It was last represented in the Duma in 2007, although it still sends deputies to local and municipal legislatures.
It is also opposed to the war in Ukraine. This Duma ballot is the first parliamentary poll since the full-scale invasion in 2022. Yabloko’s single-sentence manifesto calls for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace. A decision not to let the bearers of that message participate even in a rigged ballot suggests nervousness about the popularity of a “special military operation” that was supposed to last weeks but is now well into its fifth year, with no end in sight.
Ukraine’s use of long-range missiles and drones to attack infrastructure deep inside Russia has made it hard for Moscow to downplay the scale of the war on their doorstep or shield civilians from its consequences. The reality of fuel shortages and inflation penetrates the wall of propaganda. So does loss of life.
The true number of Russian casualties is hard to know, but is thought to be about 1.5 million, with hundreds of thousands of fatalities. In the absence of volunteers, army recruiters are increasingly turning to coercion, press ganging or tricking people into signing up. There are rumours, denied by officials, that a mass mobilisation of reserves – unwilling cannon fodder – is coming once the election is out of the way.
So it is hardly surprising that the Kremlin has abandoned what was left of its flimsy pretence of permitting dissent. The machinery for delivering an election result to the president’s satisfaction is well oiled. There is no reason to think that it will fail this time. That doesn’t make the vote irrelevant. Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians, but he cares about the appearance of being supported by them. The harder the Kremlin is seen to work at constructing electoral proof of that support, the less confident it looks.

articles.title: Yemeni army says more than 20 airstrikes hit Houthi targets in central Yemen
articles.body:
Ahmed Khalifa and Tarek Chouiref
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
The Yemeni army said Saturday that more than 20 airstrikes hit Houthi positions and military assets in the central Al-Bayda province, inflicting heavy losses.
The strikes targeted Houthi positions, gatherings, vehicles, missile launchers, and a communications system in the districts of Al-Zahir, Dhi Na’im, Al-Sawadiyah, and Mukayras, according to the Yemeni Armed Forces Media Center.
The military said the attacks caused heavy personnel and equipment losses but provided no figures.
Separately, the government-aligned Giants Brigades said it shot down a Houthi first-person view (FPV) attack drone before it reached its target.
The group did not specify where the drone was intercepted or what it was targeting.
The Houthis have not commented on either claim.
Earlier Saturday, the Yemeni army said its warplanes struck dozens of Houthi trucks carrying weapons, ammunition, and missiles from Taiz toward Sanaa, the Houthi-held capital.
The developments come amid intensified fighting across Yemen, with the Houthis reporting gains along the western coast. Government forces said they have advanced in the northern Al-Jawf province and carried out strikes on Houthi positions in Taiz, Lahj, and Al-Dhale.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

articles.title: Houthis claim missile, drone attack on Saudi military base
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi group has carried out an attack using ballistic missiles and drones against a military base in southern Saudi Arabia, the group announced.
In a statement posted on X platform, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the attack targeted weapons depots and command-and-control facilities at the Sharurah military installation.
Saree stated that a large barrage of ballistic missiles and unmanned aircraft was deployed, claiming the strikes successfully hit their designated targets.
He framed the attack as direct retaliation for ongoing Saudi military strikes on Yemen, warning of expanded attacks deeper inside Saudi territory should air strikes persist.
Saudi authorities have not formally commented on the claims regarding the Sharurah base.
However, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence reported earlier on Saturday that a projectile landed in Al-Tuwal governorate in the southwestern Jazan region, injuring two people and causing material damage to a mosque, several residential buildings, and civilian vehicles.
Shifting front lines
The strikes coincide with significant shifts across Yemen's territorial map amid escalating clashes between government forces and the Houthis since July, which ended years of relative calm.
According to the group, the Houthis now control the entirety of western Al-Hudaydah province following advances in western Taiz province, where they captured the strategic coastal city of Mokha and its Red Sea port.
The advance has placed Houthis in close proximity to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most critical maritime choke points.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces have made territorial gains in the northern Al-Jawf province along the Saudi border, advancing toward its provincial capital, Al-Hazm.
Active combat also continues across contested fronts in Marib, Al-Bayda, and Al-Dhale provinces.
Yemen has remained gripped by conflict since the Houthis captured the capital Sanaa and large swathes of the country in 2014, prompting the military intervention of a Saudi-led coalition in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukraine’s military logistics – MOD (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russia hits Ukraine’s military logistics – MOD (VIDEO)
Russian forces have struck logistics and energy facilities supporting Ukraine’s army, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said, adding that some attacks hit railroads used to bring military cargo from the EU.
In a statement on Sunday, the ministry said that a group strike involving high-precision weapons and drones attacked “logistics centers through which military cargo is supplied and distributed.” Among the targets was a Nova Poshta logistics center in Odessa Region used for military purposes and two power substations in Odessa and Nikolaev regions that supported local port logistics.
The ministry added that railway facilities in western Ukraine were also struck, noting that they were used as routes to move military cargo from European countries.
Ukrainian officials claimed that the overnight raid involved more than 450 drones across the country.
Odessa Region Governor Oleg Kiper confirmed the barrage, saying that it had damaged warehouses, as well as a residential building and several private homes, with fires breaking out at several locations. He said preliminary information indicated no casualties.
Footage on social media, meanwhile, showed what was described as a massive fire at the Nova Poshta warehouse.
In Ivano-Frankivsk Region, western Ukraine, Governor Svetlana Onischuk said that a drone attack damaged an industrial facility and an apartment building. Separately, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported that a logistics warehouse in the Borispol district not far from Kiev also came under attack.
The new barrage comes as Ukraine has intensified long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia, targeting critical infrastructure, oil refineries, and civilian facilities, including e-retail warehouses. Moscow has retaliated by attacking Ukraine’s defense industry and military-related facilities, and maintains that it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Kiev strikes emergency fuel convoy to Europe’s biggest nuclear plant – Rosatom
articles.body:
Kiev strikes emergency fuel convoy to Europe’s biggest nuclear plant – Rosatom
Ukraine has carried out a series of strikes on tankers delivering emergency diesel fuel to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), killing two Russian servicemen and wounding multiple others, Rosatom CEO Aleksey Likhachev has said.
The attacks took place on Friday in the immediate vicinity of the plant’s perimeter and targeted fuel trucks transporting diesel needed for the facility’s emergency power systems, Likhachev said in a statement on Sunday.
Two Russian servicemen were killed and “a large number” were wounded, some seriously, according to the Rosatom chief. He said the troops had been involved in securing a “strictly civilian mission” to maintain fuel deliveries to the nuclear facility.
Likhachev accused Kiev of knowingly targeting the tankers despite being aware of their cargo and its importance to nuclear safety.
The incident comes just days after the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) warned that the ZNPP’s diesel reserves had been critically depleted during nearly three weeks without external electricity. The plant lost its sole remaining power connection on August 20 and had to rely entirely on emergency generators until a temporary IAEA-brokered ceasefire allowed repairs to be carried out and the line to be reconnected on September 7.
Even after external electricity was restored, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi stressed that replenishing diesel remained essential because the plant could again lose grid power due to unspecified “military activity” in the area.
During the latest blackout, the plant had reduced the number of operating generators from four to two to conserve diesel and began running some cooling pumps intermittently. The generators provide electricity for essential safety systems, including pumps cooling all six reactors and their spent fuel pools.
Likhachev accused Kiev of deliberately increasing the risk of a nuclear emergency at Europe’s largest nuclear power plant.
“The Kiev regime has openly embarked on a path of provoking a nuclear incident at Europe’s largest nuclear power plant, with unpredictable consequences,” he said, arguing that any such event could affect areas far beyond the immediate vicinity of the facility.
The Rosatom chief called on the IAEA to “strongly condemn” the attack and explicitly identify those responsible. He also urged Kiev’s Western backers to distance themselves from what he described as the Ukrainian government’s “most horrific crimes.”
The IAEA has repeatedly warned about military activity around the ZNPP and nearby Energodar. In its latest update before Likhachev’s statement, the agency reported hearing explosions, drones and sustained gunfire in the area and said the plant’s power situation remained “increasingly fragile.”

articles.title: Yemen government forces say they hit Houthis in Red Sea city
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen government forces say they hit Houthis in Red Sea city
Yemen's Riyadh-backed government forces said on Saturday that they had struck Houthi fighters in the strategic Red Sea city of Mocha.
Following a week-long offensive, the Houthis on Friday captured Yemen's Red Sea coast, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the US-Iran war.
They had seized Mocha the day before after heavy fighting.
"The armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime" near Mocha's port, the government news agency Saba reported on Saturday.
The spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they had also struck Houthi vehicles and fighters on the Mocha-Dhubab road, just outside the city, according to Saba.
Nazili said on Friday that government forces had begun shelling areas in Mocha, and called on citizens not to use the Taiz-Mocha and Mocha-Dhubab roads.
The fall of the city to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
On Friday, Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha's airport, while a local official said the city's seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
News site Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had twice called US President Donald Trump to request American strikes on the Houthis last week.
But on Saturday, Trump told reporters that "the Houthis called us and they don't want to fight with us".
He didn't say if Washington would take action, but added "everything's gonna work out fine and dandy" in the region.
The United States previously conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis, starting in March 2025, in response to the group's repeated attacks on international shipping in support of Hamas in the war on Gaza.
That effort ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel.
More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis' ground offensive, launched last week, has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 76,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Saturday, a figure that had quadrupled since last week.
Yemen's civil war began with the group's takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014, and was paused by a 2022 truce that fell apart in July.

articles.title: Trump urges Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian diesel supplies
articles.body:
Yasin Gungor
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
US President Donald Trump urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to halt military strikes against Russian diesel refineries, warning that the operations are creating global fuel shortages.
 
"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told reporters, adding: "Let him go after targets, but not diesel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel."
 
The US president said that current disruptions across diesel markets do not stem from tensions in the Middle East but rather originate from the war between Russia and Ukraine.
 
Trump said Washington raised the matter directly with the Ukrainian leader, emphasizing that American officials do not want Kyiv targeting refineries.
 
Ukrainian forces have "plenty of other targets" available for military strikes, Trump said, arguing that destroying Russian diesel production capacity is "hurting the world."
 
Ukrainian officials have not issued an immediate response to the US president's statements.
 
Kyiv escalates drone campaign against refineries
 
Trump's appeal comes as Ukraine sharply intensifies attacks against Russian energy hubs and refining infrastructure. On Sept. 10, Zelenskyy said that Ukrainian units hit eight military-supporting facilities within 24 hours, including an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region and a seaport in Dagestan. Strikes also targeted the Novorossiysk naval base and oil terminal on Sept. 9 and processing complexes across Ryazan, Perm, and Tatarstan on Sept. 7.
 
The sustained disruption has constrained Moscow's ability to process crude into transportation fuels. In response, Russia introduced diesel export curbs in July and extended them through September.
 
Iran, after US-Israeli strikes that began in February, announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to navigation, causing widespread disruption to global energy and trade flows.
 
Recent attacks by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia's oil pipeline have further strained the market.

articles.title: Train carrying Boris Johnson and Merz adviser evacuated near Polish border in Ukraine due to Russian drones
articles.body:
Boris Johnson and Merz adviser's train stopped near Polish border for evacuation due to drone attack, but all-clear given
German newspaper Der Spiegel has learned that passengers on a train carrying Günter Sautter, one of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's closest advisers, security advisers from other European countries and former UK prime minister Boris Johnson were woken and prepared for evacuation near the Polish border following an attack on another Ukrainian train. The evacuation did not take place, however, as the all-clear was given after no further drones were detected.
Source: Spiegel, citing sources; Carl Bildt, former Swedish prime minister, on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to information obtained by Spiegel, Sautter was travelling by train from Kyiv to Poland on the night of 12-13 September. At around 05:00, the train stopped near the Polish border; some passengers were evacuated from the train due to drone strikes in the border region.
The security measures were prompted by an incident on the same railway line, where a Kyiv-Warsaw train was also targeted by a drone near the Polish border in the early morning. The state-run railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) reported that the locomotive of the train was struck, but no one was injured.
Sautter was in the Ukrainian capital alongside security advisers from the UK, France and Italy, as well as representatives of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's government, to discuss possible peace negotiations with Russia. On 13 September, he attended the international YES conference on security.
In addition to Sautter, the train also carried security advisers from other European governments, members of the German Bundestag, diplomats and academics.
Former UK prime minister Boris Johnson also travelled to Poland on this special train after the conference.
No passengers were injured. The train stopped after a drone alert, prompting conductors to wake passengers and evacuate them. The all-clear was given shortly afterwards after no further drones were detected.
Bildt explained that passengers were instructed to evacuate, but the order was cancelled and the train was able to continue its journey.
Robin Wagener, a member of the Green Party in the Bundestag, was also on board the special train. The MP expressed his outrage following the attacks.
"These drone attacks are blind terror against the Ukrainian civilian population and a dangerous escalation of Putin's war," Wagener told Spiegel.
The parliamentarian views the attacks as a provocation against Ukraine's supporters.
"Russia is becoming increasingly unprincipled and is playing with fire right on the border of the European Union and NATO; we must finally put a clear end to this terror," Wagener stressed.
Background:
- Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated that the Russian attack complicated his team's crossing of the Ukrainian-Polish border.
- Dariusz Sinecki, spokesperson for the Nadbużański Border Guard Unit in Poland, said that a drone hit a lorry near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing on the night of 12-13 September.
- Earlier, Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said that the Yahodyn border crossing itself on the border with Poland had not been hit.
- Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that there had been no violation of the country's airspace.
- Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this was Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin's terrorism, which is "knocking directly on the doors" of the EU and NATO.
- Ukrzaliznytsia reported that Russia had struck the locomotive of a passenger train near the border with Poland.

articles.title: Moscow expects new round of trilateral Ukraine talks in foreseeable future: Kremlin spokesman
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Moscow expects a new round of trilateral talks on Ukraine to take place in the foreseeable future, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Sunday.
Speaking in an interview with the Russian daily Izvestia, Peskov said the option of holding such a meeting was discussed during the recent contacts.
“As for the trilateral meeting, this has been discussed. We hope it will take place in the foreseeable future. In this regard, we are on the same page as (US envoy) Mr. (Jared) Kushner,” he said.
The official added that there were currently no new proposals on the table, but said the purpose of the trilateral meeting would be to look for new options.
“As for whether there are any new proposals — there are none at the moment. But that is precisely what the trilateral meeting will be for -- to look for some new options,” he noted.
Commenting on a statement by Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had previously said that the deployment of European troops to western Ukraine would amount to war with Russia, Peskov said it was a general warning about the consequences.
“He spoke in general about the mistakes that are being made and could be made, which is prompting Europeans to think about some political alternative,” he said.
Commenting on calls by Poland to step up NATO exercises near the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, Peskov said Russia is taking measures to ensure its security.
“The fact that NATO is gathering and conducting military activity there is clear. Therefore, we are taking all necessary measures to ensure the security of this important Russian region,” he said.
Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorskiy said earlier that NATO should increase its exercises near the border with the Kaliningrad region.
In a separate statement, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan confirmed to Putin that the UAE is ready to provide a venue for talks on Ukraine.
“The Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi confirmed that the Emirati side is ready to provide its venue, as it did before,” he said.
The comments came after US President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv last week as part of efforts to revive negotiations on Ukraine.
Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5, with the Kremlin describing the talks as “substantive, constructive and useful.”
The following day, they traveled to Kyiv, where they held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The US envoys said the discussions were “substantive” and expressed hope for renewed momentum in the peace process.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Hit Near Polish Border, Kyiv-Warsaw Train
articles.body:
Russian forces launched strikes near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing along Ukraine’s western border with Poland on Sunday morning, Sept. 13, damaging a filling station and hitting the locomotive of a passenger train en route to Warsaw.
The bombardment struck within two kilometers of the Polish border in the Volyn region, sparking a sharp diplomatic warning from Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who described the cross-border escalation as Russian terror “knocking directly at the doors of the EU and NATO.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Volyn Customs spokeswoman Valentyna Chernysh, falling munitions ignited a blaze at a commercial gas station complex and engulfed several parked freight trucks nearby.
State Border Guard Service (DPSU) spokesman Andriy Demchenko confirmed that incoming fire did not directly hit the border inspection infrastructure itself, though operations at the Yahodyn crossing were temporarily halted during the air raid alert while personnel and travelers sheltered.
The crossing subsequently resumed normal processing operations once the immediate threat subsided.
Concurrently, state rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia reported that Russian munitions struck the locomotive of a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw approximately two kilometers from the Polish border.
Rail monitoring teams detected the incoming threat and issued an advance warning to the crew, averting casualties among passengers and rail staff.
Russian Strikes Injure 12 Across Odesa, Ternopil, and Konotop
Sybiha demands full Western embargo
Sybiha condemned the morning strikes, warning that Moscow is deliberately testing the boundaries of allied airspace and border security.
“Barbaric Russian strikes near the Ukrainian-Polish border in Yahodyn are not simply a continuation of attacks on Ukraine’s state borders. This is Putin’s terror knocking directly at the door of the EU and NATO. The Russian barbarians are already at your gates, dear partners,” Sybiha stated.
Sybiha appealed directly to Western allies to impose sweeping, non-incremental economic penalties to hold the Kremlin accountable.
“Act now: bring the full power of your sanctions against Putin’s aggressive regime,” Sybiha urged. “Make Moscow feel the consequences of its terror. Not partial decisions, but decisive and powerful steps: a full trade embargo, a total entry ban, and complete sanctions against the military-industrial complex.”
Persistent targeting of transport and fuel infrastructure
The border assault marks a further geographic expansion in Russia’s sustained aerial campaign targeting Ukraine’s transportation corridors and energy distribution networks.
On Saturday, Sept. 12, Russian strikes hit railway infrastructure in Fastiv, Kyiv region, and the western regional center of Lutsk, prompting Ukrzaliznytsia to evacuate passengers and railway staff.
The operator also truncated direct rail service to the northeastern city of Sumy, rerouting passenger journeys to Konotop and substituting bus transfers due to recurring attacks on rolling stock.
Earlier in the week, Russian strikes targeted four passenger trains across the Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, and Kharkiv regions over a 48-hour span, killing three people and injuring 20 others.
The damage to the filling station near Yahodyn also coincides with an escalating campaign against retail fuel networks across Ukraine.
On Saturday, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced that the government is testing automated early warning software to alert gas stations to incoming drone flight paths following deadly strikes on multiple fuel complexes in Kyiv that killed two people and injured four on Friday.
