articles.title: German lawmaker says his train escaped Russian drone attack by chance
articles.body:
Ayhan Simsek
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
German lawmaker Robin Wagener said Sunday he had been traveling by train on the same line hit by a Russian drone attack near the Polish border, warning that Russia was an “immense danger to Europe’s security.”
In a social media post, the Green lawmaker said he had just come from Kyiv, where air defense fire and drone attacks were more intense than on previous visits. “And this morning I traveled by train on the same route where this attack happened,” he wrote, sharing a video of the strike. “Sometimes chance decides whether you get through safely — after Russian terrorists have already decided on the attack.”
“Russia is an immense danger to Europe’s security. Too many of us have still not realized that,” Wagener wrote. “Our support for Ukraine in defending against it is still too hesitant.”
In the German parliament, Wagener serves on the Foreign Affairs and European Affairs Committees and is the Green group’s spokesperson on Eastern Europe. He also chairs the German-Ukrainian parliamentary friendship group.
German weekly Der Spiegel reported that a special train traveling from Kyiv toward Poland with former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European officials aboard was stopped early Sunday because of a drone threat. Guenter Sautter, one of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s closest advisers, was among those on the train. Parts of it were evacuated after drone strikes in the area.
The security measure followed an attack on the same railway line. Early Sunday, a drone struck a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw near the Polish border. The operator said the locomotive was hit. No one was injured.
Sautter, a foreign and security policy adviser at the Chancellery, had been in Kyiv with security advisers from Britain, France and Italy for talks with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s government on possible peace negotiations with Russia. He also attended the Yalta European Strategy conference on Saturday.

articles.title: Yemeni government forces strike Houthi positions, down 5 drones
articles.body:
Mohammed Sameai and Sahin Demir
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Yemeni government forces said Sunday they carried out airstrikes against Houthi positions, personnel, and military equipment and shot down five drones belonging to the group amid escalating fighting across the country.
The Yemeni Armed Forces’ media center said army aircraft conducted three strikes on Houthi positions and barracks in Al-Taba Al-Sawda and Jabal Al-Munim on the Al-Dhabab front in southwestern Taiz province.
The army-affiliated September Net website separately reported that air forces targeted Houthi personnel, equipment, and vehicles in the coastal city of Dhubab and on northern fronts.
The strikes destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed Houthi fighters, the report said, without providing casualty figures.
In a separate development, the government-aligned Nation’s Shield Forces said its 6th Brigade shot down five Houthi drones in the Al-Aghbara area on the Al-Wazi’iyah front west of Taiz during clashes.
The developments come amid major changes in territorial control in recent days as fighting between government forces and the Houthis, which intensified in early July, continues.
The Houthis have announced taking control of several districts in the western coastal provinces of Al-Hudaydah and Taiz, as well as islands in the Red Sea, including Mayyun Island in the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Government forces, meanwhile, have reported advances in the northern Al-Jawf province near the Saudi border and said they were approaching the provincial capital Al-Hazm.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

articles.title: Watch first naval battle in history fought entirely by drones: Ukrainian uncrewed boat spots, fires on, and sinks Russian one in Black Sea
articles.body:
For the first time, two unmanned boats have fought a battle at sea, and the Ukrainian one sank its Russian rival. The Ukrainian Defense Intelligence has spotted a Russian drone in the Black Sea, and a Sargan-3000 naval drone armed with a remote-controlled machine-gun turret opened fire and destroyed it, the Ukrainian Navy said on Telegram, calling it "the first-ever naval battle between unmanned boats."
Drone-versus-drone combat has moved from the sky to the sea. Ukraine has already rewritten naval warfare with uncrewed boats, sinking warships and pushing much of Russia's Black Sea Fleet back to port without a navy of its own to speak of.
Now it has fought and won the first duel between two robot vessels, a glimpse of automated sea combat. The claim is the Navy's. It released a video of the encounter but did not provide a date, an exact location, or the type of Russian craft, and it has not been independently verified.
A gun turret decides the duel
The Russian vessel was detected by units of the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence, the Navy said, before the Sargan-3000 closed in.
The Ukrainian drone carried an automated 12.7mm Protector remote weapon station, a turret of the same type mounted on some NATO warships, and used it to sink the Russian boat.
The published footage shows the two drones engaging and the Russian craft going under.
The Sargan-3000 reaches far
The Sargan-3000 is a Ukrainian multi-purpose strike drone that passed combat testing in April. It has a combat radius of up to 1,600 kilometers, runs at 40 to 55 knots, and carries up to 450 kilograms of payload, according to Militarnyi.
It is the same class of boat that sank the Russian border patrol ship Izumrud near Novorossiysk in July.
Ukraine keeps rewriting naval war
The battle fits a campaign that has reshaped the Black Sea. Ukrainian sea drones have sunk the corvette Ivanovets (link) and the landing ship Caesar Kunikov (link), in 2025, even shot down a Russian Su-30 fighter jet (link), and in the last ten weeks alone struck 285 vessels of Russia's shadow fleet (link).
Russia is now racing to build its own uncrewed fleet, and satellite imagery suggests it is constructing a dedicated naval-drone port in occupied Crimea, a sign that the sea, like the sky, is filling with machines that fight each other (link).

articles.title: ‘Escalation is becoming a fact’: Tusk says Russia may target Ukrainian border crossings after drones hit a Kyiv–Warsaw train and nearby gas station

‘Escalation is becoming a fact’: Tusk says Russia may target Ukrainian border crossings after drones hit a Kyiv–Warsaw train and nearby gas station
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk held a special briefing after Russian forces launched drone strikes just a few miles from the Ukrainian-Polish border. On the morning of September 13, one drone struck a gas station a few miles from the border, while another hit the locomotive of a passenger train.
“The escalation of actions by the Russian Federation is becoming a fact, and examples of it are ever closer to our border,” Tusk said. (All quotations in this article are from the Polish Press Agency.)
Tusk said he believes Russia will try to intensify its operations in Ukraine in the coming weeks and months. “We unfortunately cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory,” he said.
Tusk said the Russian military may seek to disrupt operations at Ukrainian border crossings and perhaps even destroy them, which could directly affect Poland.
Tusk expressed hope that “this worst-case scenario will not materialize” and said the Polish authorities would do everything possible to protect the country. He also said Poland was prepared to ask its NATO allies for help if necessary.
Tusk said that in the strikes, the Russian military used new jet-powered drones whose range and accuracy “are worrying.”
Overnight on September 12–13, Russian forces launched drone attacks on a gas station near the Yahodyn border crossing and a passenger train on the Kyiv–Warsaw rail line. Two people were injured in the strike on the gas station, Suspilne said. No one was injured in the strike on the train. The train crew had received a drone warning and evacuated the passengers. Another train carrying Western politicians returning from Ukraine was near the train struck by the drone. Russia’s Defense Ministry said the strikes had targeted “railway infrastructure facilities used to transport military cargo from European countries.”

articles.title: Ex-CIA officer caught with $40 mn in gold bars seeks plea deal
articles.body:
Ex-CIA officer caught with $40 mn in gold bars seeks plea deal
The US Justice Department has reached a tentative plea agreement with an ex-intelligence officer suspected of faking a classified CIA assignment to steal more than $40 million in government-provided gold bars as “work-related expenses.”
David Rush, who once worked as a senior CIA official with top-secret clearance, was arrested in May after an internal probe discovered he had lied about his education and Navy service. A search of his Virginia home uncovered a trove of 303 one-kilogram gold bars, some $2 million in cash and 35 luxury watches.
Rush has so far been formally charged only with theft of public funds for falsifying pay records to obtain around $77,000 in military-leave compensation. The case has not yet been presented to a federal grand jury.
In a joint motion filed on Friday, Rush and federal prosecutors said they had reached a “plea agreement in principle” and asked the court to extend the indictment deadline from September 17 to October 8, giving them another 21 days to resolve the matter.
“The parties need additional time to prepare the paperwork,” Assistant US Attorney Raizza Ty and Rush’s attorney, Jessica Carmichael, wrote in the filing. “A pre-indictment resolution promotes the public interest by conserving government and judicial resources.”
The document did not disclose what charge Rush would plead guilty to or any possible sentencing recommendation. The parties said proceeding with an indictment and trial would require extensive litigation involving classified material. A deal could avert a public trial and keep key details of the case under wraps.
The court filings said that, beginning last November, Rush requested and received “a significant quantity of foreign currency and tens of millions of dollars in gold bars for work-related expenses,” but official details remain scarce. According to media reports, Rush invented a special-access “continuity of government” operation, ostensibly intended to preserve federal functions during a nuclear war or other catastrophe.
The case has also prompted officials to scrutinize US Deputy Secretary of Defense Stephen Feinberg, a private equity billionaire who reportedly oversees the Pentagon’s $33 billion military intelligence budget. Earlier this week, NBC News reported that Feinberg had recommended Rush for sensitive assignments and praised his performance to senior CIA officials. The outlet also said footage showed both men at a government-affiliated residence used by Rush.
Feinberg has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the Pentagon has denied he endorsed Rush for any position, describing reports of a close professional relationship as “false and embellished.”

articles.title: Brics hammers out joint declaration after India bridges Iran-UAE chasm
articles.body:
PM Modi and other Brics leaders at the 2026 summit in Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi
NEW DELHI: In a dramatic repeat of the 2023 G20 Declaration under India’s presidency, Brics member-states reached a consensus for a joint declaration following intensive, late-night negotiations that lasted till 4 am on Saturday. The talks had been strained by sharp differences between the UAE and Iran over the West Asia conflict and an earlier meeting of the Brics foreign ministers under India’s presidency had ended without a consensual statement.Also Read | Iconic moments, landmark talks & a breakthrough pact: Key points from Brics SummitThe 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration announced by PM Narendra Modi was solidified by a rare leader-level Iran-UAE meeting - between Iran President Masour Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan – in the middle of the war that started on February 28.
In a delicately worded compromise, the declaration addressed the interests of both sides by expressing serious concerns over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and also peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), in violation of international law and relevant resolutions of the IAEA. This implicit criticism of US-Israeli action against Iran was crucial in getting Iran to sign off on the declaration.
Zero tolerance for terror, Pahalgam gets mention
“We in Brics must fight against the normalization of attacks on civilian, vital infrastructure. The same applies to peaceful nuclear infrastructure," said Pezeshkian at the summit.Nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm, said the declaration.Significantly, the joint statement did not name any country or explicitly condemn attacks, prioritising instead dialogue and diplomacy, UN Charter, civilian lives and infrastructure and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of all States, while also expressing deep concern over continued escalations and calling for maximum restraint.Also Read | 'India can be bridge-builder': UN hails Iran-UAE meeting on sidelines of BricsIn the declaration, the leaders recalled their respective national positions on West Asia and stressed the need to work together to maintain smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law.Official sources said India led prolonged negotiations at multiple levels to reconcile sharp differences between the 2 sides and forge consensus with support from other member-states who were keen that the summit didn’t end without a joint statement.The Brics consensus is reminiscent of the last-minute G20 2023 Delhi declaration that was achieved in the middle of the escalating Russia-Ukraine war with a carefully nuanced formulation that called upon all States to refrain from use of force for territorial acquisition but without naming Russia.The Brics declaration also came days before Iran’s meeting with GCC countries on the Strait of Hormuz situation. In Pezeshkian’s meeting with the crown prince, the leaders underscored the importance of supporting efforts to ease tensions, promote de-escalation and strengthen regional stability.Indian officials had on Friday expressed confidence about a constructive outcome from the negotiations, following Modi’s meeting with Pezeshkian in which he expressed solidarity with Tehran, seeking a long-term and win-win partnership with Iran.On other issues, like in Rio last year, China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterated their support to the aspirations of Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Importantly for India, the declaration expressed strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as “criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed” and strongly reiterated condemnation of the Pahalgam terrorist attack.“We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens,” said the declaration.On the Palestine issue, Brics countries, including India, expressed deep concern on the continued violence in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreement of October 2025. “We call for halting any policies aimed at forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza Strip and express concern regarding arrangements that may prejudice the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and legitimize or prolong occupation,” said the declaration.
There was no mention of the Ukraine war in the declaration this year. The declaration backed comprehensive reform of the UN, including the Security Council, with a view to making it more “democratic, representative, effective and efficient” and to increase the representation of developing countries in the Council's memberships.

articles.title: Hegseth pressed rescued F-15E crew for CBS interview
articles.body:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and senior officials in his department pushed for the two crew members of an F-15E shot down over Iran in April to appear on CBS’s “60 Minutes” and recount their rescue operations, CNN reported, citing several sources familiar with the matter. The sources said the two crew members initially expressed reservations about appearing on the program, with one even raising concerns that he could be explicitly ordered to take part in the report.
At the same time, three of the sources said military officials were concerned that classified details about the rescue operation could be disclosed. The sources said senior Defense Department officials insisted that the crew members be interviewed, but after the two voiced concerns, Hegseth met with them and asked them directly whether they wanted to participate rather than forcing them to cooperate. Following the conversation, according to the report, one of the crew members, identified by the call sign “Bravo,” agreed to be interviewed, while the other, identified as “Alpha,” refused.
CNN said its latest report highlights how the Defense Department under Hegseth has sought to shape the narrative surrounding the war with Iran as public criticism of the administration over the issue grows.
“This entire story is a complete lie,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in response to CNN’s questions about the report. “The decision to participate in the interview was each pilot’s alone — because it is their story.”
“The Department took great care to ensure operational security, sources, and methods were protected,” he added. “To suggest otherwise is to denigrate every member of our military who participated in and supported the interview.”
Iran succeeded in shooting down an F-15E in April, the first U.S. fighter jet downed in the country during the war. Two crew members, a pilot and a weapons systems officer, were aboard. The pilot was rescued hours after ejecting from the aircraft, while the weapons systems officer managed to evade capture by Iranian forces in the mountains for more than a day before he too was rescued.
CNN also reported on the battle among media outlets seeking interviews with the two crew members since their aircraft was shot down, saying “the competition was intense.” According to the network, a “60 Minutes” producer contacted military sources on the day of the rescue in an effort to secure the interview. The program’s executive producer told staff that landing the interview was a “top priority,” and according to three sources who spoke with CNN, she dealt directly with Hegseth and other senior administration officials in an effort to secure an exclusive for the program.
As noted, the report said military officials were concerned about details being disclosed while the campaign was still underway. Two sources who spoke with CNN said active-duty service members expressed concern that featuring the incident on the program was an attempt by the Defense Department to use the heroism of U.S. troops in the successful operation for political purposes. According to the sources, political appointees at the department insisted that the interview go ahead despite those reservations.
According to one source familiar with the production of the program, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine also expressed concern that the interview could reveal military tactics, even inadvertently. He ultimately decided to participate in the report himself.
In the first preview of the interview aired by the network, “Bravo” is seen sitting silently as the interviewer asks him: “Did you ever have any doubt that the US military was coming for you?”

articles.title: Peace Through Strength NOW!
articles.body:
The following is a press release from the organizers.
The 22nd Annual Meeting of the Yalta European Strategy (YES) “Peace Through Strength NOW!” was held on 11-12 September in Kyiv. 700 leading politicians, diplomats, businessmen, servicemen of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, veterans, civil activists, and experts from 28 countries took part in the YES conference organized by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Opening the event, Victor Pinchuk, businessman and philanthropist, founder of YES, said:
“Peace through strength is about immediate action, immediate action by Ukraine, Europe, the United States and other partners. The Ukrainian will to fight has been superior from the start. Ukrainian innovation has become superior in 2026. Exactly because of this double superiority, the window of opportunity has appeared — a window of opportunity to force our enemy to sit down for serious and real negotiations to end the war. But windows of opportunity are very rare and fast disappearing.
This is why we need our partners to give even more military and financial support, invest more in Ukrainian defense and sanction our enemy more to decrease its resources. And, most importantly, this winter Ukraine must have the most protected sky in the world.”
Introducing the artwork created especially for the conference by the world-famous British artist Banksy, Victor Pinchuk said:
“One work expressed most what the title of the conference means. World-famous artist in 2022 went to the small town Borodyanka, 30 miles from Kyiv. Russian destroyed his houses and tried to capture Kyiv. There he sprayed on a wall a work which became iconic — a small child who flips to the floor a big judo fighter who thought he was a master. And this great artist, who never shows himself, created a new work especially for our conference. And this is his first ever self-portrait in such a scale.
For me, Banksy in this picture symbolizes all our Western partners. He is here like they are — always with us, always standing with Ukraine. And of course we all understand this small child is Ukraine. Peace through strength, Ukraine style.”
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky stressed in his video address to the participants of the Annual Meeting: “It is very important today not to lose any time and to strengthen our daily efforts to ensure the defense of the country.”
The President of Ukraine underlined that developing Ukraine’s own defense capabilities, defense industry and partnerships is a critically important part of the country’s long-term security guarantees, both during the war and in the post-war period.
“It is vital to build our own system shielding our skies, and not only that. We will need it during the war, of course, and afterwards, because part of Ukraine’s security guarantees is the Ukrainian army, our production capabilities, our capacities and our partnerships with Europe, the United States and Canada,” Volodymyr Zelensky stressed.
He emphasized that security guarantees are peace guarantees, and it is peace that Ukraine needs most of all. He urged for focusing on the present-day challenges Ukrainians face every day.
“Security guarantees are guarantees of peace, and peace is what Ukraine needs so much.”
The President of Ukraine thanked the participants of the YES 2026 Annual Meeting for supporting Ukraine and demonstrating that Ukraine is not alone in this fight.
“I am very pleased that you have such a distinguished gathering; I understand that everyone has come to support the conference. At the same time, the Yalta conference is one of the building blocks of the broader support being provided to Ukraine. Every such conference, every such meeting, in my view, is very important in order to demonstrate to Ukrainians that they are not alone in facing the enemy. And secondly, it is important to demonstrate to the Russians that no one will abandon Ukraine until there is a just peace. Thank you,” Volodymyr Zelensky concluded.

articles.title: US envoy Kushner: If Ukraine agreed to give up territory demanded by Putin, we would already have a deal
articles.body:
US envoy Kushner: If Ukraine agreed to give up territory demanded by Putin, we would already have a deal
US President Donald Trump's special envoy Jared Kushner has said that the only thing missing for an agreement to end the war is Ukraine's consent to give up its territories within the boundaries demanded by Russian ruler Vladimir Putin.
Source: Kushner at the annual YES forum in Kyiv on 12 September
Details: Kushner said Washington had already prepared most of the peace agreement, but its signing is being held up by Ukraine's unwillingness to make territorial concessions to Russia.
Quote: "President Putin's laid out his line of what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that. And obviously, our job as the mediators [is] to figure out how can we come up with a creative solution that doesn't violate their desires and that helps them achieve their objective, and does in a way that we can get Russia to end the conflict in a way that hopefully allows both parties to move forward in a framework where this doesn't happen again." [N.B. Ukrainska Pravda does not recognise Putin as president – ed.]
Details: Kushner also said that the mediators' task is to find a "creative solution" that would allow the conflict to be frozen. At the same time, he believes the territorial issue should be resolved based on the situation on the battlefield.
In his address, the US president's envoy avoided mentioning Russia's perpetration of genocide in Ukraine, instead focusing on rhetoric that equated the losses suffered by both sides. He claimed that both Kyiv and Moscow are experiencing "a lot of pain" and have "a lot of desire" to end the war.
Quote: "At least for now, they [the Russians – ed.] are saying the right thing, which is they want to discuss a way to resolve this in a way… President Zelenskyy is very committed to this, from what we've seen. From what we heard, President Putin is very committed to this as well. We have to find the right formula that hopefully works for everyone to advance it forward."
Details: During his address, instead of addressing Russia's responsibility for its unprovoked aggression, Kushner proposed focusing on business interests and "better prosperity and economics" after the fighting ends.
Significantly, while he was discussing Putin's readiness for genuine peace talks, an air-raid warning was in effect in Kyiv amid another Russian attack.
When asked how often he plans to visit Kyiv to demonstrate support and help bring about at least a temporary halt to air strikes, Kushner said he prefers to work remotely.
Quote: "We're not really into performative diplomacy. We do what we need to do on the phone, we do what we need to do over Zoom… I'd love to come back when we have peace."
Background:
- On 6 September, the US president's special envoy Steve Witkoff said the task of the US delegation that visited Kyiv and Moscow was to "bring the sides closer together".
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that three rounds of talks had taken place on 6 September and that all of them had been "very substantive"; they addressed possible parameters for ending the war and support for Ukraine in the short term.
- Kushner said at the time that an end to the war in Ukraine before winter is not guaranteed, but that the US side is working to create the conditions to achieve this goal.

articles.title: Zelenskyy calls on EU to sanction Usmanov and Fridman: Russian oligarchs should not be treated as friends
articles.body:
Zelenskyy calls on EU to sanction Usmanov and Fridman: Russian oligarchs should not be treated as friends
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on the European Union to increase sanctions pressure on Russian businesses, including by imposing sanctions on Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Details: Zelenskyy noted that since the morning of 12 September, Russia had launched almost 500 strike drones against Ukraine.
"Essentially, the Russians have expanded this war from the front lines, where they cannot achieve success, into the economy, and their tactics are as primitive as they get – destroying every facility that can help people withstand the conditions of war," he added.
Quote: "Russian businesses that pay taxes into the war budget, and Russian oligarchs without whom Putin's system is impossible to imagine, must feel that there is no place in the world where they can live in peace and quiet for as long as this war continues.
When the Ukrainian economy is simply a target for Russia, this is certainly not the time for Europe to treat Russian oligarchs as friends. When Russia uses every euro and dollar to prolong the war, it is both immoral and suicidal to give Russian businesses opportunities to live their lives without feeling the consequences of the war."
Details: Zelenskyy said "Usmanov and Fridman are exactly the kind of Russian business figures who need to find the courage to take concrete steps against the war".
Quote: "With 500 Shaheds a day, this is certainly not the time to even begin the discussion about easing sanctions – especially sanctions against individuals about whom no one can say how exactly they have helped protect lives and reduce Putin's ability to continue the war.
We need to keep up comprehensive pressure on Russia for its war. Strengthen sanctions against Russia instead of weakening Ukraine!"
Background:
- On 11 September, EU ambassadors once again failed to agree on extending personal sanctions over Russia's aggression because of Slovakia and France's demands to change the list of sanctioned individuals.
- The deadline for extending these sanctions is 15 September.
- The restrictive measures targeting individuals were last extended on 14 March. On that occasion Slovakia also pushed until the last minute for Fridman and Usmanov to be removed from the list.

articles.title: Rapid Houthi gains in Bab el-Mandab put Israel on alert as Red Sea threat grows
articles.body:
The Houthi offensive in Yemen is drawing close attention from Israel’s defense establishment as the new Jewish year begins, with officials increasingly concerned by developments around the Red Sea and their potential implications for global shipping and Israeli security.
In recent days, the Iran-backed Houthis have continued capturing towns along the southern Red Sea coast and gained control of the Bab el-Mandab Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime trade routes.
The dramatic shift came after forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government withdrew from the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, which sits in the middle of the southern entrance to the strait. The withdrawal effectively gave the Houthis a critical position from which to exert control over the waterway.
Officials in Jerusalem have described the development as concerning, but Israel’s defense establishment is not expected to intervene unless Israel itself comes under direct attack.
The Houthi takeover and their gradual expansion across the maritime region are viewed in Israel as more than a localized development. Israeli defense officials see the situation as potentially dangerous not only for Israel but for countries around the world that depend on the shipping route.
The geography makes Bab el-Mandab particularly vulnerable.
Farther north in the Red Sea, near Yemen’s major port city of Hodeidah, the sea is relatively broad, ranging from about 160 to 260 kilometers (100 to 160 miles) across. But farther south, at the strait itself, the waterway narrows to only about 18 kilometers (11 miles).
That difference is significant from a military perspective.
By comparison, the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has demonstrated its ability to severely disrupt maritime traffic, is about 55 kilometers (34 miles) wide. Israeli security officials believe controlling or disrupting shipping could be considerably easier at Bab el-Mandab, which at its narrowest point is roughly one-third as wide.
In such a confined waterway, sophisticated radar systems or other complex surveillance capabilities are not necessarily required to identify and target ships. Vessels can potentially be observed visually, while relatively simple weapons, including Kornet anti-tank guided missiles, could be fired at them. Explosive-laden boats could also be dispatched against passing vessels.
Israeli assessments therefore suggest that control of Bab el-Mandab could allow the Houthis to select targets with considerable precision, potentially giving the group substantial leverage over a maritime route critical to the global economy.
Questions in Israel over collapse of deterrence
Behind closed doors, some Israeli officials are sharply criticizing what they view as a collapse of deterrence in the region and questioning why Saudi Arabia, Yemen’s internationally recognized government and other regional actors have not responded more forcefully to the Houthi advance.
The result, in their assessment, is that the Houthis have gained the upper hand while encountering relatively little resistance. The developments have also exposed what some Israeli officials view as serious shortcomings in the military flexibility and capabilities of the forces expected to confront the Yemeni rebels.
That weakness stands in contrast to the Houthis’ determination and willingness to employ virtually any means available while their opponents retreat.
The concern within Israel’s defense establishment is that if the Houthis successfully exploit their control of Bab el-Mandab, a more cohesive and formidable Iran-led regional coalition could emerge — one that another power may eventually have to dismantle.
For now, U.S. President Donald Trump has refrained from intervening directly.
“The Houthis don’t want to fight us,” Trump said Saturday, addressing the escalating tensions.
Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice last week and asked the United States to strike the Houthis. Trump has so far rejected the request.
Israeli Navy raises readiness
Against the backdrop of the latest developments, the IDF has adjusted its readiness.
Alongside protecting Israel’s land borders, the military is strengthening efforts to defend strategic assets at sea and preserve freedom of navigation for Israeli shipping.
Navy commander Vice Adm. Eyal Harel has ordered the service to raise readiness across its command-and-control network. Senior commanders have also reinforced naval forces at sea in an effort to prevent surprises in the maritime arena.
From the IDF’s perspective, developments in the Red Sea are part of a much broader transformation of maritime security that could ultimately extend into the Mediterranean.
The maritime arena has undergone dramatic changes, from Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz to the Houthis’ latest gains around Bab el-Mandab.
Israeli officials believe armed groups across the region have closely watched Iran’s actions at sea and that Tehran’s successes have whetted the appetite of its allies to use maritime areas for their own operations. The concern is that such activity could escalate from provocations into serious violations of freedom of navigation and, in some areas, effective control of strategic waterways.
For Israel, the stakes are particularly high.
Although it has land borders, Israel is heavily dependent on maritime commerce and is often described by its security establishment as functioning economically like an island. About 98% of its imports by volume arrive by sea, making uninterrupted access to maritime trade routes a strategic necessity.
As a result, Israeli defense officials increasingly view the sea as a central theater of national security.
Ensuring freedom of action at sea and guaranteeing the movement of goods to and from Israel can no longer remain merely policy slogans, officials say. Those commitments must be backed by greater military capabilities.
The conclusion taking shape within the defense establishment is that the Israeli Navy will have to expand and significantly strengthen its capabilities in the coming years if it is to meet a maritime challenge stretching from the Mediterranean through the Red Sea and into some of the world’s most strategically important shipping lanes.

articles.title: Israeli troops in Syria call for 'conquest of Damascus'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli troops call for 'conquest of Damascus' amid continued attacks on Syrian territory
Israeli reservists have called for the military to expand its illegal operations deeper into Syrian territory, with a senior officer saying many troops would favour advancing as far as Damascus, according to Israeli media.
Reserve officers serving with the Israeli army's 210th Division have criticised limits on the scope of its operations in southern Syria and called for increased activity inside Syrian villages and surrounding areas, Israeli news site Walla reported.
The officers reportedly argued that deeper incursions would help push what Israel considers potential threats further away from its border.
A senior Israeli officer defended the military's current approach but acknowledged the appetite among reservists for a more wide-scale invasion of Syria.
"Would the reservists like to conquer Damascus? Many of them would," Walla quoted the officer as saying.
The issue was also raised during a visit by Israeli military chief of staff Eyal Zamir around two weeks ago, according to the report.
The officer said reservists deployed to Syria often arrived after serving in Gaza and Lebanon, where the operational environment was significantly different.
"What is happening today in Syria is beyond anything we imagined and any activity we thought of - the activity is non-stop," he said.
Israel currently operates from 10 military positions inside Syrian territory, according to Walla, conducting operations around the clock based on intelligence and military assessments.
The report said Israeli forces have conducted raids well beyond the immediate border area, singling out Beit Jinn in the western Damascus countryside, around 11 kilometres from the occupied Golan Heights.
The senior officer said some reservists wanted to reach Beit Jinn "every day", saying that 14 militants had been killed in three separate Israeli raids in the area.
The comments come amid continuing Israeli military operations around Beit Jinn and elsewhere in southern Syria.
Israeli forces carried out a series of incursions in the Damascus and Quneitra countrysides on Saturday, sources told The New Arab.
An Israeli force comprising two tanks, a bulldozer and more than 10 other vehicles entered agricultural land surrounding the Beit Jinn farm area in the western Damascus countryside, according to the sources.
Another force of three military vehicles entered an area west of Saida al-Hanout in the Quneitra countryside, while four Israeli military vehicles entered the town of al-Rafid, where soldiers searched several homes.
Israeli forces also fired an artillery shell at agricultural land in the Ain al-Shaara area near Beit Jinn following similar shelling overnight.
Israeli military operations have become increasingly frequent in southern Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime in December 2024.
Israel moved troops into the UN-patrolled buffer zone separating the two countries following Assad's fall and has since established military positions and carried out raids, arrests and strikes deeper inside Syrian territory.
Syria and the United Nations have said Israel's deployment violates Syrian sovereignty and the 1974 Disengagement Agreement governing the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces.
France on Friday called for Israeli troops to withdraw from Syrian territory, while reiterating its support for efforts to reach a security agreement between Damascus and Israel.
The French foreign ministry told Syria's official SANA news agency that any military deployment within the separation zone constitutes a violation of the 1974 agreement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has condemned Israel's violations of Syrian sovereignty, saying Damascus had received support from more than 40 countries at the UN Security Council.
He reaffirmed Syria's territorial integrity and said it would continue defending its rights through "all legitimate political and diplomatic means".
A UN commission investigating Syria said earlier this week that Israeli military activity in the country's south had become "increasingly sustained and entrenched", warning that some Israeli actions could amount to war crimes.

articles.title: Russia Fired 2,100 Drones and 78 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian forces launched approximately 2,100 strike drones, 78 missiles of various types, and nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Sept. 13.
Zelensky emphasized that a substantial portion of the unmanned aerial vehicles deployed in recent days consisted of high-speed, jet-powered Shahed drones, which Moscow utilized to systematically batter Ukraine’s domestic economy, critical utilities, and civilian life.

“Just this week, Russia has launched about 2,100 drones against Ukraine,” Zelensky stated.
“A significant portion of them are specifically jet-powered Shaheds, with which the Russians are trying to break the economy and destroy people’s lives. The enemy also used almost 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 78 missiles of various types.”
Weekend assaults on railways, energy, and border infrastructure
The president highlighted that overnight and early morning bombardments on Sunday struck national energy facilities, the Ukrzaliznytsia railway network, commercial enterprises, and residential buildings across multiple provinces.
In the southern port city of Odesa, Russian forces carried out sustained combined missile and drone strikes that damaged residential high-rises, warehouses, and a botanical garden, injuring at least five civilians.
Zelensky noted that emergency and utility crews were actively conducting restoration operations across numerous western regions following overnight strikes.

He referenced emergency interventions underway in the Volyn region near the Ukrainian-Polish border, where falling munitions damaged a commercial filling station and Russian fire struck the locomotive of a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw just two kilometers from the frontier.
The border strikes in Volyn coincided with drone impacts on transport and industrial infrastructure in the western regional center of Ternopil, as well as strikes on residential property in Konotop, Sumy region, injuring civilians across both locations.
Containing the threat to European borders
Framing the escalating aerial onslaught as an acute challenge to the broader European security architecture, Zelensky warned that the international community must recognize Russian strikes near allied borders as a shared threat requiring decisive joint action.
“It is precisely to prevent these strikes from going further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and prevent aggression from expanding,” Zelensky emphasized.
“Russian terrorism is a common threat to many, but it can and definitely must be defeated in Ukraine.”

articles.title: Russian drones target Volyn, Rivne oblasts in rare mass attack in western Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a mass drone attack on western Ukraine on Sept. 12, injuring at least five people in Volyn Oblast and causing power outages in neighboring Rivne Oblast, regional authorities said.
Both regions are located in Ukraine's northwest, far from the front lines, making them less frequent targets for Russian attacks.
The attack on Volyn Oblast lasted more than four hours, with more than 10 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles entering the region’s airspace, according to regional Governor Roman Romaniuk.
Most of the drones targeted the Kovel community, Romaniuk said. Five people were injured and received medical assistance. No deaths were reported.
Debris from one of the drones also struck a passenger train in Lutsk. Passengers had been evacuated before the impact, and no one aboard was injured, according to the governor.
In neighboring Rivne Oblast, Russian attacks caused power outages in parts of Dubno and in the Rivne district, according to regional Governor Oleksandr Koval. An unspecified enterprise in the Sarny district was also destroyed in the attack.
No casualties were reported, and energy crews were working to restore electricity, Koval said.
The attacks illustrate Russia's ability to strike deep into western Ukraine, far from the line of contact. Volyn borders Poland and Belarus, while Rivne lies immediately to its east.
Western Ukrainian regions have repeatedly come under long-range Russian drone and missile attacks targeting energy, transport, and other infrastructure. While these regions are targeted less frequently than Kyiv or Odesa — and far less frequently than front-line cities in Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts — they have increasingly been reached by Russian drones during large-scale nationwide attacks.
On Sept. 3, Russian drones hit several western regions during a nationwide attack that killed five people and injured dozens.
The attacks on Volyn and Rivne were part of a wider Russian drone assault across Ukraine on Sept. 12. According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia launched nearly 500 strike drones at the country during the day.
"In essence, the Russians have expanded this war from the front lines, where they cannot achieve success, into the economic sphere, and their tactics are extremely primitive: to destroy every object that can help people endure the conditions of the war," Zelensky said.

articles.title: Only Roland Garros towel left, says Ukraine tennis player after Russian strike hits flat
articles.body:
Only Roland Garros towel left, says Ukraine tennis player after Russian strike hits flat
- Published
Ukrainian tennis player Dayana Yastremska has said her family's flat has been destroyed in a Russian aerial strike on the Black Sea port of Odesa.
"This is what the 'Russian world' looks like. A direct hit by a Kalibr cruise missile," she wrote on social media, showing a photo of a burning multi-storey residential building.
"The only thing that survived was a Roland Garros... towel," the 26-year-old added, posting an image of a famous clay orange towel from Paris's Grand Slam tournament hanging from the wreckage.
Odesa regional head Oleh Kiper said 37 people were injured, including a baby, and two missing in the missile and drone attack on Odesa and nearby Chornomorsk on Friday night.
"A Russian missile destroyed our apartment in Odesa... SYMBOLIC. A piece of world tennis survived a Russian missile. Our home did not," Yastremska wrote on Instagram on Saturday.
"@wta @itf_reviews Look at these images through our eyes," she said in a reference to the governing bodies of world tennis - the Women's Tennis Association and the International Tennis Federation.
Yastremska - who in 2024 reached the semifinal stage of the Australian Open - is currently 113th in the women's world singles rankings.
It is not the first time Ukrainian athletes' homes have been hit by Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Last year, Ukraine international football midfielder Heorhiy Sudakov said his flat in the capital Kyiv had been severely damaged by a Russian drone while his wife and child were at home.

articles.title: Russians seek answers over hundreds missing after Ukraine's 2024 incursion
articles.body:
Russians seek answers over hundreds missing after Ukraine's 2024 incursion
- Published
"I used to have complete faith in our country," says Lyubov. The last time she spoke to her mother was a day after Ukrainian forces broke into Russia's Kursk region more than two years ago.
Now she feels "resentful towards the [Russian] state", in a country where most people avoid criticising the full-scale invasion unleashed on Ukraine in February 2022.
The local governor says more than 300 Russians are still missing in Kursk region, but no-one really knows the true figure.
Lyubov says she tried to persuade her mother to leave her village in the Sudzha area, but blames Russian state TV "propaganda" for her refusal to listen. Some 2,000 people remained in the settlements captured by Ukraine's military, Russian authorities estimate.
"The state channels were convincing viewers that 'everything is under control: two or three days, and it'll be just as it was before'," she recalls.
She still fails to understand why Russian authorities could not stop Ukrainian soldiers storming two border checkpoints in August 2024, taking around 40 prisoners and bombing a convoy carrying Russian soldiers.
Within six days they had overrun more than 777 sq km (300 sq miles) of Russian territory, as Ukraine's military sought to divert Russian forces away from their front-line offensive.
For most of the next eight months, mobile and internet links were down.
Russia's foreign ministry repeatedly accused Ukraine of war crimes against civilians: allegations rejected in Kyiv as completely unfounded.
Nearly 200 Russians sent a letter to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the United Nations, asking them to organise a humanitarian corridor to evacuate civilians.
It never happened and, by late autumn, battles raged as Russian forces sought to retake the territory.
Lyubov and others who had lost contact with their loved ones began to form groups.
One resident, whose family friends had also stayed behind, began compiling a list of people she saw on videos published by the Ukrainian military and journalists. Then she began detailing those believed to have died and where they were buried.
"At first, in a panic, you try to do something – anything – to find some sort of information," she said. "Taking action brings a certain sense of relief, and that's how you can cope with the stress."
Soon about 1,000 names were on the list.
Lyubov wrote to the Red Cross and Kursk interior ministry appealing for help, but had no response.
Early in 2025, Russia's human rights commissioner published a list of 517 Kursk residents reported missing. The list mixed up names of the missing with those who were searching for them, and the families said it was like a "slap in the face".
"Publishing something like this is the height of incompetence and a lack of basic respect for people," said one young woman whose parents had gone missing, in a video shared online.
Heavy fighting had been reported in late 2024 in the village of Darino, where Lyubov and mother were from, and authorities said that 90% of it had been destroyed.
The Russian military regained control of the village and then began evacuating those who had survived, and the bodies of those who had not.
One of the evacuees got in touch with Lyubov, telling her she had lived with her mother for the past few weeks. Her mum had passed away, she explained, following a head injury in circumstances that remain unclear.
A few other elderly people had also died, she said, unable to cope with wartime conditions.
Lyubov waited in vain for her mother's body to be brought out, while other families had no idea if their relatives were alive or dead.
People complained no-one was searching for their loved ones and that there was no single list of those missing.
Lyubov heard that the bodies of neighbours who died alongside her mother had been taken away from Darino in April, but her mother's body was still missing.
She tried and failed to get an answer from the authorities: "They wouldn't listen, and everyone just kept saying that it was dangerous there, and no-one was going to deal with it right now."
The head of one local village council, Yuri Tkachev, was among volunteers who went to retrieve the bodies of civilians, from the streets or from nearby fields.
"It's hard for people to know – or rather not to know – what has happened to their loved ones, whether they're being held captive or have died, and where they died," he said.
Body bags and fuel for vans taking part in the evacuations were paid for either by the volunteers themselves or with donations, but not by authorities.
Although regional officials met the group searching for the missing several times in the second half of 2025, relatives complained it made little difference.
Lyubov was still searching for her mother's body, until she visited the mortuary last October during a trip to the regional capital Kursk.
"I just asked: 'A woman born in 1949 from the village of Darino – are there any unidentified bodies?'"
The official turned his laptop screen towards her and immediately she recognised her deceased mother in a photograph from April 2025.
She was lying on her side in the street, her knees bent. Lyubov tried not to look too closely. She recognised her mum's face and an old jumper, which she wore while she worked.
She had provided a DNA sample in January but was told it had been lost, so her mother's body had been in the mortuary unidentified for several months.
She had wanted to bury her mother in their home village, but for now that is impossible, so she has been cremated and her ashes sit in Lyubov's apartment in Belgorod, about 100 miles away.
She is bitter that the government failed to stop the incursion, that it did not evacuate residents when it could, and that it persuaded them the situation was not serious.
Asked by the BBC to comment on this story, there was no response from the Kursk governor, Russia's human rights commissioner or the Russian Red Cross.
The command of Ukraine's Territorial Defence Forces and Ukraine's human rights commissioner of Ukraine said all the civilians they had evacuated from Kursk region had been handed over to Russia.
Lyubov thinks back to when she used to ride her bike across the border into Ukraine to shop for sausages, yarn and ice cream.
"We went to see them, and they came to see us. And now not one of these villages exists any more."

articles.title: Part of workshop destroyed: OSINT analysts reveal damage to Russian chemical plant from Flamingo missile strike
articles.body:
Part of workshop destroyed: OSINT analysts reveal damage to Russian chemical plant from Flamingo missile strike
OSINT analysts from the Exilenova+ community have released satellite imagery showing the consequences of a strike on a Russian speciality chemicals plant in Volgograd. A Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile destroyed part of a workshop at the facility.
Source: Exilenova+; Fire Point, Flamingo's manufacturer
Details: Exilenova+ explained that Ukraine's defence forces struck the Volgogradpromproekt plant on the night of 10-11 September. A missile hit the plant's main workshop.
"One of the FP-5 missiles completely destroyed a 20x15-m section of the main workshop," Exilenova+ stated.
The use of the Flamingo missile was confirmed by its manufacturer Fire Point. According to the company, the FP-5 completely destroyed an annex building.
"As a result of the strike, a building covering approximately 380 sq m completely collapsed and was destroyed," the company said.
Meanwhile, the OSINT analysts reported that one of the missiles did not reach the plant. A crater from a Flamingo strike was recorded near the facility in Volgograd.
The Volgogradpromproekt plant specialises in speciality chemicals, producing organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants, resins and other chemical components for industry. Its products are used in Russia's aviation and shipbuilding industries and the defence industrial base.
The plant produces ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts and develops chemical production technologies.
Background: On the night of 11-12 September, Ukraine's defence forces attacked the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara Oblast. The plant supplies Russia's military-industrial complex.

articles.title: Europe should impose sanctions after every massive Russian strike, not wait for packages – Sybiha
articles.body:
Europe should impose sanctions after every massive Russian strike, not wait for packages – Sybiha
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this at a joint briefing with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski in Kyiv on Sunday, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"We discussed once again the approach that we should not wait for large sanctions packages, but after every massive strike on Ukraine, adopt relevant sanctions packages against the aggressor – against Russia – including an 'Anti-Ballistic Package'," he said.
Sybiha added that Ukraine's partners should deprive Russia of its ability to manufacture ballistic missiles and drones and restrict its access to military technologies. According to him, there is still significant potential in this area.
"Unfortunately, Russia has learned how to circumvent sanctions. Unfortunately, Russia continues to use components of products manufactured in Western countries, in European countries, in the production of both ballistic missiles and drones. And we have provided this information to our European partners," the diplomat said.
As reported, a bill to strengthen sanctions against Russia, which the U.S. Senate approved by an overwhelming majority last month, will be put to a vote in the House of Representatives next week.
